div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

A Much-Travelled PrineeSs.—Princess Louise Augusta of Schleswig-Holstein, is shortly going to the East again, though not in connection with the visit of .the Prince and Princess of Wales to India. Like her mother Princess Christian, she is food of foreign traveehaving already visited many of the British possessions in the East, and she is the only one of our Princesses who hes travelled in America. She was married in 1891 to Prince Aribert of Anhalt. and while living in Berlin or Potsdam, saw much of her cousins,the German Emperor and Empress. Since the dissolution of her marriage, five years ago, she has divided her time between foreign travelling, and leading a quiet life at home, near her parents and elder sister,Princess Victoria,to whom she is greatly attached. Her Royal Highness is very popular in Society,and has a sweet and kindly nature which makes her adored by all her friends. Her most trusted com- panion is the Hon. Mary Hughes, who was maid of Honour to Queen Victoria from 1891, until the death of her Royal Mistress in 1901, and afterwards acted as lady-in-waiting to the Princess. Madame Melba.—The autumn opera season at Covent Garden is a comparatively new feature in London social life, and is Attracting large and fashionebler audiences. Chief among the artistes is Madame Melba, than whom there is no more delightful singer. Australia is naturally proud of her, for she was a Miss Nellie Mitchell, and was born at Burnley, a suburb of Melbourne. She was sent to the Melbourne Presbyterian Ladies' College,and is best remembered by her schoolfellows as a wonder- ful whistler :ether than as a singer. Afterwards she became the principel soprano at the Roman Catholic Cathedral. Her father, Mr. David Mitchell who is still living, and is a Presbyterian of the old fashioned school did not object to her holding this position for several years, but he was strongly opposed to her becoming a professional vocalist. She however became well-known as a concert ball singer in Melbournesafter her marriage with Captain Armstrong, but her father never would hear her sing in puhlic until she revisited Melbourne some three years ego. Women and the Real Work of the World.—The meeting of the " National Union of Women Workers " will take place at Birmingham next week. These annual conferences are held in different towns each year, but. there are., few: more convenient for this purpose, or in which women workers arc -engaged to a greater extent -in industrial life Virtu in the great Midland city. That the workers take great interest in the discussion on thel carious problems of lire is evidenced by the large numbers of women who are ready to pay for tickets to : hear them at, these annual coeferencee. The subject discussed are not as a. rule of much interest to those brought up in idleness, and the rnetters to be considered next week mostly refer to the housing, training, educe- lion, recreation, conditions of labour, and emigration of the classes who carry on the real work of the world. The latter subject. will be Approached from different standpoints. bv at least half-a-dozen speakers, under the presidency of Lady Aberdeen, who, as an ex-Colonial Governor's wife, takes a special larest in this particu- lar subject. The Coming of Christmas.—Already we are being reminded or the approach of the festive season. The Post (Mee has issued its usual notice .regarding the early posting of Christmas cards for the Colonies. and the shops are also beginning to display the legend " Suitable for Christmas gifts." For those who have neither friends or relatives to send abroad, there is plenty of time as yet to be thinking of Christmas shopping, but it is ale-aye well not to leave this until the rush comes and many of the best things have been snapped up. As regards Christmas cards the publishers say that the demand is as great as ever, hut it is certain that the plain greeting card is steadily displacing those of the pictorial description. The Queen who has her cards speniarly prepared, usually strikes a happy medium between the two extremes, arid as a rule her Maiesty's Christmas cards bear a reproduction of souse famous picture for which she has an especial fancy. Bridge Prizes.---It was Lord Brougham whom the King has recently honoured with a visit at Brougham Hall, who introduced Bridge into this country. At present the game is as pcpuler as ever, and the search for suitable prizes is often as battling as the bunt after Christmas and wedding gifts. Clocks are played oust, so also are the cut glees bottle with silver tops' button hooks, shoe-horns, hair brushes, purses, and photo frames, and hostesses desirous of expending only a moderate sum in this direction,- are frequently at their wits end. Even when one knowsahe taste of the person for whom a 'gift is intended, the selection is by no means easy. but when it is uncertain whether a man or woman is to receive it, and with not aghost of an idea Which man, or which woman of ORO'S party will be the recipient, the guest is readered very much more diffi- cult. Jewellery is selected by many Society hostesses, richly bound hooks are another favonrite choice, and again beautiful little pictures often firore among Bridge prizes, when the cest thereof has not to be seriously considered. . . . .

Concerning 11airdres3ing.—Foreheads are corning in They are not, in the majority of instances becoming but they are the fashion, and are therefore being cultivated by the smart set. The wise among us how- ever, unless possessed of really pretty foreheads, will do well to retain a few soft fluffy curls, and remain con- tent with being better to look upon, if less fashionable. The ladies of our Royal Family, rarely if ever change their mods of hairdressing, end many of our genic/ dames are noted for the original and picturesque dress- ing of their tresses. Lady nranby -for example is invariably seen at evening functions with her hair. just tucked into a diamond sewn not. while Lady Lytton may he seen wearing a diamond ribbsn threaded through her simply arranged coiffure. When, a liamess to a beautiful ancestress is marked and unmistakable, many a smart IV0,11:111 nowadays adopts the style of hair- dressing patronised by the said ancestress, indulging In as few modifications as possible. . Chiffon Velons.—The demand for chilTon-verous is greatly exceeding that for any otter kind of velvet, and as a matter of fact, this exquisite fabric .is by no means the extravagant ,vear soms people represent it to be. Of course it needs careful treatment, but given this. chiffon velours by no means comes undsr the catgory of those fabrics deserving of the title " fragile wetr." Moreover chiffon velous lends itself most amiably to the dyeing process.Tn the matter of drapingmo nutteriat

has yet been discovered to equal it, even the softest and most exquisite cashmeres are far behind in this special direction. Usually chiffon velous is sold in very wide widths and therefore the cost of a gown or wrap is less than it would appear to be, at a first glance. Our Uncurable Colds.—Autumn colds are just now prevalent to the point of vulgarity, and there are few things which the doctors seem to know less about than a "cold in the head." • There was recently an toter- national conference at Liege, to discuss the right and proper method in which to bring up a baby. One would have thought that conference to be unnecessary in this the twentieth century, but there are some things upon which, in spite of the experience of ages, and the boasted advance of medical science, and civilisation' the world remains in a state of primitive ignorance, and one of them is the curing of an ordinary cold.. There are hundreds of recipes and so-called remedies, but not one of them is to be relied upon as an effective cure. Very few doctors claim to do moro than alleviate its symptoms, and in this case the King gets no more help from science than the poorest of his subjects. It affects loth rich and poor alike, and it is remarkable that it has never occurred to distinguished sufferers to use their influence 'Cot- the summoning of an inter- national congress upon "How to Cure a Cold in the Head."
MADGE.

A FAMOUS FINNISR ACTREI'S. The Finnish theatrical world has just ens- tained a severe loss in the death of Frit:dein, Emilie Bergborn, a native actress and literary genius, who has passed away at Helsingfors. This lady, who was born in 1334, at Wasa, was the daughter of. a Finnish Senator, and .her re- markable talents drew the atte4on of all lite- rary Finland to her early in life. For thirty years she stood in' the forefront of her country's artistic life, and it was only last year that she retired from the scenes of her public life.

SMART REDINGOTE COSTTME. More and more popular grow the fashionable redingote costumes. The long coat gives dn additional amount or warmth that will be very acceptable when the cold weather comes. Then, too, the long sweeping- lines make for grace and elegance when the wearer is tall and slight enough to make this mode becoming. Pictured in our sketch is a smart little costume of this kind. The material of which it is

fashioned is a fine smooth cloth of the grey tone known as elephant. The long coat has a roll back collar of velvet in a deeper shade. Filling up the front is a smart little vest of white cloth braided with grey silk braid min- gled with a touch of gold. The cuffs on the gigot sleeves are of the same velvet as the collar. The skirt is quite • plain and very full round the hem. The coat fastens by means of three enormous buttons of mother-o'-pearl. A hat of pale-blue felt trimmed with feathers and velvet is worn• with the costume. A NEW TRADE IN LONDON.

'For years past, writes a correspondent, the Artistes Stoppedrs have been known in Paris. ! but 'the first of their characteristic blue and white signboards has just appeared in London, ' naturally in a French quarter.' An Artiste Stcppeur. to put it baldly, is a woman who ' mends holes in cloth. If moth-holes come in a , valuable gown, if a dress-coat gets torn, if a nail makes an ugly tear in a dainty twill skirt, a Parisian takes the spoilt garment to the •nearest stoppeur, who deftly mends the hole so that the place where the rent was cannot be de- tected. If a heartrending stain will not yield tct ordinary measures, the stoppeur cuts out the offending spot and fills the hole with her own work, which can only be compared to wearing.. Her charges are fairly high: that is to say, she asks seven or eight shillings for mending a three- cornered tear in a silk voile skirt, but afterwards the skirt that under ordinary conditions could only be an eyesore is ready to face the world without a flaw on its deliciite surface. To mend an uncomfortable little tear on a man's coat ! costs three or, four shillings, and a clever stoppeur will renovate a checked waistcoat that has been burnt by a lighted match so that not even with a Magnifying glass can one tell where the hole has been. SIMPLE WINTER BLOUSE.

No apology is necessary for bringing before the notice of our readers yet another design for a simple winter blouse. If a skirt of the same material were made to wear with it, it would make a trim little costume for the business girl, whose requirements oecupied our thoughts a short time ago. This blouse bodice can be made in such a variety of fabrics that it is useless to fix on one as being more suitable than another.

It is not necessary to have it lined. though of course lined blouses look better and wear better than those that lack a lining; but the little front should be made on a lining yoke, with a tape passing under the arms, by which simple means the front can be made safe and neat looking. Note the novel little vA,..lvet tie, which is just drawn through a -silk-covbred ring before disap- pearing under the blouse, this touch of velvet being repeated in the buttons and in the belt.

div.head: WOMAN'S NEW FiuußE.
div.p: WOMAN'S NEW FiuußE.

It is a curious coincidence. writes a • Path correspondent, that the papers have chronicled the death of Auguste Person. the inventor of the crinoline, and the birth of the Directory as the coming mode. Whether it has been launched with sufficient authority or not I do not know. but a Directoire gown was worn • the other after- minti at a repetition generale by one of our most popular actresses. The master who presides over the making of the mode has decreed that the feminine figure is not as it should be. It is too pronounced; it needs Softening and rounding off. This is the object of the new fashion in which I the female form divine is suggested rather than ! stated explicitly in whalebone. The story is that three ladies who had lost some of the slimness of youth were responsible for the vogue of the crinoline. Presumably. the Directoire period will be equally useful to those who wish to simu- late a figure that is not strictly theirs. At any i rate, it has a grace and a charm----an effrontery even—which does not belong to those fearsome compounds of steel and cambric of the Second Empire: and no one could imagine the crinoline! in a motor-car.

div.head: DIPHTHERIA AND .MANURE HEAPS.
div.p: DIPHTHERIA AND .MANURE HEAPS.

Dr. Ferraud traces the relation between Manure heaps and rural epidemics of diphtheria. On one occasion the disease appeared the day following a general street cleaning. He argues that manure should be kept in closed wells Of stone, glazed with bitumen, so constructed thar the fluids filter away from the solid matter.

div.head: TEMPERATURE OF ADULTS.
div.p: THE TEMPERATURE OF ADULTS.

The ordinary .temperature of an adult when a i thermometer s placed under the armpit is 98.4 deg.; in the mouth, 99.5 deg. The blood is about 100 deg. Blood heat is marked on the thermometer at 99deg.Fahr. In fevers this is much exceeded; and the heat of the patient may rise to 105 deg. to 106 deg.; a higher temperature than this will generally prove fatal, unless it de- scends very quickly. The highest temperatures recorded have been in some cases of rheumatic fever, when that of the body rose to 109 deg., and even to 111 deg.

div.head: SEEDS FROM PREHISTORIC •PLANTS.
div.p: SEEDS FROM PREHISTORIC •PLANTS.

One of the oddities of a coal mine in Belgium is that the earth brought to the surface with the coal contains many seeds of plants unknown to modern botanists. .As the shaft runs to a depth of 126 ft. it would seem that these seeds must be those of plants which flourished ages ago, which, after centuries, of darkness, at last spring into growth when again brought to the vivifying influences of light and air. Most of the products are rank growths of weeds unlike any of the latter-day- segetation, and they form a curious study for the botanist, who has vainly sought for their twentieth century descendants.

div.head: CASTOR-OIL AND DYEING.
div.p: CASTOR-OIL AND DYEING.

Within comparatively recent years. that is, since aniline dyes have almost completely sup- planted the mineral and vegetable dyes formerly used in colouring cotton textiles, an extensive demand for castor-oil has sprung up in the in- dustry of dyeing and printing cotton goods. Without presuming to invade the intricacies of the dyer's art wherein secret recipe, for the composition of colours and their application to cloth are the property of each individual dyer, is may be said that the general principle under- lying the utility of this oil in colouring processes is that the aniline and alizarin° dyes are soluble in sulphtirated castor-oil; in other neutral fats and oils these dyes, with few exceptions, are in general insoluble. In certain processes of dyeing and printing, therefore, castor-oil enjoys a. prac- tical monopoly over all other oils.

div.head: VENOMOUS EMOTIONS.
div.p: VENOMOUS EMOTIONS.

Anger, fear, anxiety are among the emotions or sentiments which literally ' poison our blood, It has often been said that evil thoughts are poisonous, the meaning being that they corrupt other people, but the real fact is that they poison our own bales. By losing control of ourselves and indulging in anger. by yielding to anxiety, fear, and unwholesome thoughts, we caifse an irritation or disturbance which, according to the scientists, has the effect of producing a poison in the blood that may have serious consequences. Naturalists declare that the venom of snakes is generated by anger and fear; that it is rapidly collected in a special receptacle, and thence %dis- charged at the object of its anger or fear, and it is further explained that the same process takes place in the human body, but that we have no special organ to receive ft. and it therefore dis- perses in the blood, acting against ourselves in- stead of for our protection. Be that as it may, it is generally conceded that we are literally poisoned by the emotions mentioned, and by any sentiment or passion which up.l,ets the smooth Working of our Minds.

div.head: MYSTERY OF SLEEP.
div.p: MYSTERY OF SLEEP.

Sleep, with its -strange phenomena, remains, after the passage of thousands of years, as much a mystery as it was in the beginning of the race. Whence comes iti How produced? We as little know the answer to these questions as Adam when the deep slumber fell upon him in the garden. The craving of the body for sleep is as imperative as its cry for food. This blessed loss of consciousness is the best general medicine known. There is neither substitute nor rival for it. Sleep is the off-duty period, of consciousness. It is during this time, when the entire system is in a quiescent state, that the final processes of assimilation take place and that the body is really nourished. This assimilation is said to go on much better and more rapidly before mid- night than afterward, because of the more thorough circulation of the blood, which carries the new material and removes the waste. Oxygen, too, is consumed in greater quantities before midnight than after it. wording to the scientists, and oxygen is necessary to tho nutri- tive process.

div.head: CAUSE OF CANCER.
div.p: THE CAUSE OF CANCER.

The announcement of the discovery of the mi. crobo of cancer has been made more than once. and as often contradicted. Investigations carried out by the Royal Cancer Commission, however, seem to show that there, is no cancer microbe to discover. .The. true cause of this disease has been found to he the peculiar growth of certain cells which have forsaken their proper function. Under certain conditions, that is to say. some of the ordinary somatic cells take to multiplying after the manner of the generative cells. It is the mass formed by these body cells growing in an abnormal manner. which constitutes the can- cer. But what. it May be further asked, causes these cells to grow in this abnormal say? The only answer possible as yet is that it is the re- sult of some stimulus applied to the cells. It is to be hoped that the cause of cancer being thus far made clear some. remedy will be found in due course. This, it appears, is no. longer at any rate to be sought in the discovery of a microbe. and the preparation of an antitoxin.. In the report issued by the Harvard Medical School Commission on cancer it 'very Pessimistic note was sounded. "\Ve . are "unable," , they wrote, "to find the cause or. the origin of cancer, and we believe it will never be learnt:.

Signor Magini. an Italian electrical engineer, is said to have invented an arrangement whicll obviates some pressing difficulties in modern telegraphic communication. His system claims to "ensure perfect telegraphic cominimication even in the worst possible conditions in the electrical status of the leads." The arrange- ment consists of a transmitter and a coherer, which can be fitted into any existing system. The former consists of a small Ruhmkorft coil. into the primary circuit of which currents from the cells of a dry battery- are sent. One of the terminals of its secondary circuit is placed in communication with the lead, and the current is transformed into a vibratory, pulsating one. At the receiving station it reaches a coherer of special construction, and works a Morse or other apparatus. It is also claimed for this new coherer that it will be of great value in. wireless telmrraphy. Ma crini's system also admits of duplex telegraphing without the complicated means now employed. wbile mounted on the two extremes of the wire -no alteration of exist- ing plant is required. In submarine- work it doubles the power of the- cable, and enables two messages to be RPII t together. The currents produced by the new apparatus are .also able to jump gaps Or breaks in-Vie leads. SOCIAL SERVICE. Lecture by Ides. Cranston. Under the auspices of the Warrington Social Service League, a lecture on" Social Service in American and I,Voncinental factories and workshops "was delivered in Messrs. Crosfield's assembly room on Monday evening by Mrs. May R. Cranston (of the American Institute of Social Service). There was a large attendance over which the klv. H. Dunnico, Presideut of the League, • presided. The CiIAIRMAS Said he deeply appreciated the work which was being carried on by Messrs. Crosfield, and ' hoped the employes would support every good move- ment on the part of the firm, and thus induce 'other manufacturers to emulate their good example. (Applause.) He was glad they had Mrs. Cranston with ' than, because she ,belouged to the original institute of ' socMl Service. The American institute was the first founded, and societies had sprung up in almost every European country on the lines of the American one. (Applause). Airs. CRANSTON who was heartily received,said social • service meant baridihg together for the common interest and the common good Of humanity, and the birth i wf ' the spirit was ;witnessed in the 19th Century. She briefly sketched the inauguration and growth of the American Institute of Social Service and the formation • ot similar institutions in England and on the Continent. Social service, she said, was necessary as an act of ; self-preservation. It was no longer possible for us to • say" What are these things to me ? Am I my brother's keeper? We had to be our brother's keeper or else take the consequences. The possibilities for usefulness of those institutions were almost boundless. Their work was divided into two parts—social and industrial. In the first department the greatest question which , engaged their attention was the housing of the masses of the people. tinder the present system of slum dwellings there -must be immortality and crime. In such environments Such results were inevitable. The London County Council were the first to make a practical step in the direction of the remedying of that evil but they went to work in the wrong spirit by demolishing old houses before new odes were buil.: Liverpool was solving the problem batter than any other city as there new homes were built before the slums were destroyed. In logical sequence they were ' faced with the great question of the street child. In the United States atm in England Societies existed for the care of such children, and in the United States the problem was also forced by means of the provision of vacation schools and nurseries. Other branches of the work illustrated • by Mrs. Cranston were the ' beautifying of towns and villages and the provision of parks and open spaces. In the industrial department the work consisted of inducing employers to take an interest in those who worked for them, by making pro- vision for recreation, both indoor and outdoor, the pro- vision of ireading rooms, libraries, baths &c. As an ' instance of how employers were awakening to a sense of their, responsibilities in this direction Mrs. Cranston quoted the work of Messrs. Lever Bros., who, at Port ' Sunlight, provided- housing accommodation for their ' Workmen in addition to the other desirable items she had enumerated. ; • The lecture was beautifully and profusely illustrated by means of lantern slides and at the close Mrs. Cranston was heartily applauded for her Adress. Mr. A. H. CROSPIELD proposed a vote of thanks to Abs. Cranston and the Chairman for their services. The lecture he said had been very comprehensive, suggeStiVe and instructive. He congratulated Mrs. Cranston open havinz given them so interesting an insight into the work which was being done by the American institute of Social Service. America was developing more rapidly than any other country and if anything was taken up on that side of the water it:was not carried out by half measures. Although he knew something of what was being done by their enlightened employers he was sure they had lelrnt a great deal of what was being done e;t the other side of the water. In their centre of industry —which perhaps after £ll was not now so little—the forw‘rd movement, which he trusted the employes of the fifin would consider justified them in thinking that they in so ne degree rankedjamortg thegreat progressive firms which hart beeu mentioned that night, was doe to the initiative, eathusissm, aud energy of Dr. , Markel, backed tp by the tree, loyal and iudefatigablo work of several managers of the than, to whom they I were considerably indebted. Their indefatigable and ' übiquitous Chairman had done a great deal which was of moment in the town of %Warrington, and he congratu- ! I itecl Mr. Dennico upon his energy and pluck, and/wished ; him Godspeed in his work. (Hear, hear.) On behalf ; of the dirctols of the company he had great pleasure in expressing his sincere admiration foethe work which 1 Dr. Markel had in hand, and to hope that he would pick

up some wrinkles from the lecture which would enable him to pursue the work on well-considered lines. (Applause). Dr. MARKEL seconded. He could not help feeling that if the spirit which animated Mrs. Cranston was shared by their governing bodies and by all employers and employ& in the country, we would soon do away with slums and their corresponding vice, and with the question of the unemployed, and our lives would be better and happier. (Applause.) The vote was heartily accorded. Mrs. CRANSTON briefly responded. The Rev. IL DUN/CO in responding said he had taken , a strong stand upon social questions and introduced ; them into his pulpit because he believed that anything ; in that direction which helped to make men better was part and parcel of Christianity. That was not Christian- ity which spoke to men and left them to starve. If Christianity Wfl9 to be any use it must make men better and happier on earth. (Applause). The band, the beautiful msemby roam, and the many other remarkable social features of the works were, after all, simply effects. As logical beings, they natur- ally followed up such admirable effects to their primary cause, and when they reached that point, they could not fail to be deeply and gratefully impressed by the earnest, steady, unflagging spirit, which must have animated Dr. Markel and the other Directors of Messrs. Sir John T. Brunner, Bart., M.P. (chairman), presided at the tenth ordinary general meeting of the share- 'holders of the Widnes and Runcorn Transporter Bridge Company,held on Tuesday afternoon at the offices N 0.6, Castle-street, Liverpool. All the directors, save Sir H. Seton-Karr9 M.P. (deputy chairman), were present, together with about a dozen shareholders. The Chairman read a letter from Sir H. Seton-Karr, who wrote from Scotland that he had read with interest the report of the engineers (Messrs. John J. Webster and John T. Wood). The company's "enterprise is new of its kind, and I can only presume that the engineers' difficulties are a necessity of the case, and will be overcome by practical experience." That, proceadecl Sir John, was just what he had to say in moving the adoption of the formal report, but he had something ple)sant to add. After considering the report of the engineers, be had telephoned to Widnes to at once start the car regularly running for paying traffic. (Applause.) Dealing with the accounts, the Chairman remarked that the directors would spare no effort in the shareholders' interests—(hear, hear)—and while the , authorised capital and borrowing powers might be exhausted he did not think any creditor need be under the least anxiety, because there was not a shadow of doubt that the board would find the money to pay all that was due. The long delay in commencing business was unfortunate, but there were signs that business would not be lacking, and that the bridge would be of enormous benefit to the people on both sides of the Mersey. (Applause). A vote of thanks to the chairman closed the unani- mous proceedings. The electrical transporter oar was, we are informed, running before the close of the brief meeting. The directors have agreed to Issue a revised and more elastic list of tolls for motor-cars.

Cy GERALD BISS.
CHAPTER XVlH.—Continued
Meanwhile the Duke of Belsize sat closeted With Otto and lan Frazer in the library. _ _ _ _ .

Ever circa "Mr. Stuart's" arrival the three had been busy, discussing various details .and going through piles of 'papers, the duke talk- ing eagerly and enthusiastic-ally and Fraser supplying the points and details unobtru- sively.

Olt() had to confess himself surprised .at the extent of the plats of the conspirators and the businesslike way they had set about things. As the morning progresaed he began to find himself fired by the, duke's infectious en- thusiasm. and gradue.3ly he felt himself being drav n into the vortex of the plot.

By half an hour afier mid-day the last of the papers had been read and explained, and Fraser rose, showing his ready tact in en- deavouring to eface himself. "With your permission: sir," he ,said to Otto, "I will retire and leave You to have a private talk with the Duke of Belsize. I will return later in the day."
Otto readily assented, and Frazer withdrew. after ki locng up all the papers in a. strong box. _ . . .
"Now that .we are Licine," said the "Duke, "Jet me again .ssure. your Majesty how deeply honoured I feel by your presence in my house and your confidence in me." . .
Otto lit -a cigarette with the utmost calm- ness. He,was growing accustomed to playing at being king, and it flitted through his mind how much it would amuse Rudolph to see him in his new role.

"My dear duke," he answered in MI best manner, " I. on my side, can only thank you for my kindly reception and the great efforts you are making on my behalf. But allow me to repeat that, unless we are tog,-ther at a formal meeting of the committee, I am plain 'Mr. Stuart' to you and to everybody else." The duke bowed in assent. _ _

"Your wishes shall be respected. It is better and safer at present to ,avoid expres- sions which might cause misunderstanding, if not danger, to our plans and ourselves were they inadvertently slipped out in pnbiic." "What plans have you made for the next few days ? ' asked Otto. " To-night," replied the duke, " I thought we might dine quietly en fahiPle and give you an opportunity not only of I...cc6ming better acquainted with the duchess and myself, but of meeting my son and my danOter. 'Both of them, I may Mention, are 'en tir,:ly ignorant of the whole of our plans and ideas, and I think it is, perhaps, better that they should remain so for the present with your permis- sion."

"Certainly," agreed Otto, " if you think it advisable." "We did not take them into Our confidence atfirst," explained the older 'Man ; " and this is, perhaps, liardVr the best time to enlighten them. They might be offead.7,l •at having been kept in the dark so- -long. Let us wait until we arc nearer our goal. My daughter, who is a very charming and beautiful girl. may. I hope, play a very leading part later on."
Mr. Stuart looked up sharply, as an idea' flashed through his mind, but •he made no :otnment.

"Afterwards the Marquess and Marchioness af Swanage are giving a big ball at which royalty will be present, and I thought it might. interest you to go with our party, if you do not think that anyone will be likely to recognise you." " I do not think that there is much fear of that," said Otto quietly ; • " and I will fake care to keep well in the bactkground. I need not dance except, perhaps, with the charming Lady Sabina, if she will permit me, and I can in this way meet some of the committee socially. I should also like to show this . respect to the Marquess of Swanage." ' Excellent," said . the . "nothing could he better. To-morrow we can go into business matters again, and in . the . evening the Duchess and I are entertaining the committee to dinner at Hampstead House, after which we will hold a council under your presidency. After that we can sec what is best to be done. Next week-end, by the way, I am to entertain the other King at. Southsea Castle, my place in Hampshire; and in connection with that visit lam elaborating an idea with Mr. Frazer. But of that more later.' Shall we now join the ladies in the drawing-room before lunch? " Otto assented, and the duke led the way. The duchess and Bina we, already in the drawing-room. . • _ _

The former was very cordial to the new- comer and presented her daughter with no small pride. Bina, who had a constitutional dislike to having her hand forced, greeted Mr. Stuart with a cold and formal bow and appeared to be taken up with her father, whom she had not seen since her return.

Otto, who had been prepared in his new role to be very gracious, was inwardly rather amused at Bina's punctilioushess, realising how it would react Upon her • parents. He was, at the same time', immensely struck by her great beauty, and he found his eyes con- stantly wandering in her direction. . " A fit queen • indeed," he thought to him- self; and then he added a tumult reservation which was not so pleasant, "but she would be for Rudy." Otto was an excellent talker and had a great charm of manner and as she found that in- stead of thrusting himself upon her, he was rather inclined to ignore her, 13ina in womanly fashion began to thaw to him during lunch. By the end of the meal they were on the best of terms to the obvious delight of the duke ,and duchess. However, Bina found herself decidedly puzzled by the • marked deference which her parents paid to this strange .eommoner, the duchess especially exerting herself to be gracious. When the duke apologised tor Charlie's absence Bina fired up mentally, but she was instantly appeased by Qtto's remark that he hoped that it was only a pleasure postponed. as he was greatly looking forward to mcsting Lord Belsize. "Charlie discovered some mysllcriOns .en- gagement in the train on the wa-r. up," the said ,with a smile, "which, I fancy, may be interpreted into the club and its comzonial company. I expect he finds it more exciting than his family circle, and he ,had no• idea that we had a visitor." _

"We are all apt to undervalue home life -when we are young," said Otto a trifle sadly, "and to sigh for it as we grow older." His manner and his remark pleased Bina. " And what about your bottle, Mr, Stuart ?" she asked. " I have no real home at. present," he said gravely, " and that's why T should value one. It is the paradox of disp;ition." The duke and the duchess caught each other's eyes, and a puzzled look crossed their faces. " Oh, I'm sorry," said Bina .snftly, feeling that she had inadvertently touched a sore point, and from that moment • they were :friends. Ile setraed lonely, and that is in itself a passport to a woman's heart. Things went on more gaily, now that friendly relations had once I),Aui fully estab- lished between Bina and Otto, and the little luncheon, party grew merry, as the two chattered and laughed, cordially encouraged by the duchess, whi) unbent further than her daughter had ever seen her do before. " Fancy your not knowing London well," raid Bina, "when you know all the European capitals so intimately I" "I have only spent a very few days in London all told," explained Otto," but I hope to see more of it this time. I could not be under happier auspices," he added, bowing in the direction of his hostess. The Duchess of Hampstead murmured her thanks. "I am forced to go to the House of Lords this afternoon, I'm afraid," said the duke, who was in one of his animated moods. " would ratse-r come nr,d see Bowes of Parliament, or would you prefer my :laughter to run you round town oo.flter motor and show you the sights? She is a

very expert driver ana nas a neat nttie electric runabout car." " One can always see the Houses of Parlia- ment," said Otto gallantly,; "they are, I believe, fixtures of the Empire. But it is not given to mortals every day to drive with Lady Sabina, and if she will be so good as to take me, I can only accept with due humility and gratitude." Helooked across the table at her frankly. "I hope you have nothing better to do ? " •he said. "A stranger has no claim upon your time."
Bina had at first been decidedly annoyed at the idea of playing chauffeur and showwoman to an entirely strange young man, but his frankness disarmed her.
"But a guest of my father's has," she said graciously, "and I need hardly say that I shall be delighted." "How kind of you," he murmured, as the duchess gave the signal for rising. . . .
Half a-n hour, fa-ter the \duli'.e and duchess saw them off on their drive.

" What do you think of him, my dear ? " asked the duke enthusiastically. "Charming," replied his wife, "and se gracious. He and Bina seem to hit it off wonderfully., I ,was afraid for a few minutes in the drawing-room that she was gng to dislike him, but his manner has quite Jawed ,her." "It's a mistake to ram a man down a girl's throat," said her husband. "Let them think they did it all themselves, and they'll be happy " „ _ .
will help our plans and our wishes so," she said, smiling brightly, "if they fall in love with each other, won't it, dear ? '
, The duke 'nodded, and they separated for the afternoon to dream day-dreams and to enjoy a few pleasant hours in a fool's paradise. But that , is often worth a great deal of the prose of life.

div.head: CHAPTER XIX.
div.p: CHAPTER XIX.

CHARLIE struck up an immediate friendship with the unexpected guest, careless of his past or his future. He was a versatile youth who lived essentially in the present. In ten minutes'. time he had dragged.him off to the billiard-room to teach him the advan- tages of the pocket system over the cannon game, insisting as usual that .Bina should mark for them.

By dinner-time he had got on such terms of intimacy as to drop all complimentary and superfluous prefixes, and was calling him "Stuart," interspersed with occasional "old chap" in ' more exuberant moments. His familiarity seemed ta delight and amuse "Mr. Stuart," as much as it distressed his mother. who found herself powerless to repress his flow of conversation and spirits. . . . .

Bina looked radiant in her soft white ball- gown. and Otto thought he had never seen any woman look so lovely. Her eyes were un- usually bright, and her cheeks flushed in anticipation of the coming evening, which instinct told her would bring a change in hex whole life. She had only realised it that morning at waterloo Station, and it had been humming in her head ever since. She had taken unusual care over her toilet and had blushed at her hopes and anticipations as she took a final look at herself in the glass. She felt that she was ready to face a supreme triumph and a simultaneous surrender that great moment of paradoxical delight in a woman's life. She was full of the joy of life, and it radiated on every side of her. The (hike was at his- best, and Otto exerted hims.df to talk well, so the little family dinnet proved very bright and merry despite an undercurrent of tragedy in the hearts of three out of the five diners.

In the hall, as th,ey were preparing to start, Charlie nudged Bina. " I like this new chap Stuart," he whispered confidentially ; " he's a rattling good sort. I don't know when I've taken such, a fancy to a man for a long time." Then he added as an after thought, " Except; of course, old Ben. Which of the two do you prefer ? " The concluding question was put to tease her, and he was fully repaid by her hot cheeks and an awkward pause. "I, Charlie ? I haven't given the matter a thought, but I think they are both awfully nice." • To their visitor Bina allotted two dances, the first waltz and one later in the evening. She had wanted to reserve the first dance for some one else, but politeness demanded that she should give their guest, especially in his capacity of a stranger, the preference. She was a little surprised to notice the deference and cordiality of the greeting accorded by Lord and Lady Swanage to Mr. Stuart.

She heard her mother say: "Let me present you to Mr. Stuart, who is staying with us at present." And then both their host and hostess ad- dressed some remarks to him in a low tone, and it was obvious that they were pleased at his presence. It struck her as strange that her mother had neither apologised for bringing him uninvited nor explained who he was, but both the Marquis and the Marchioness seemed to understand.

"There is some mystery about Mr. Stuart," she ..hought to herself. ' Per,haps he is some big for.:igner travelling incopitto." But the question of Mr. Stuart's identity was soon driven out of her head, as she found herself surrounded by putative, partners, and she was delighted to see Ben Nevis in the fore. frimt. He greeted her in a low voice. "Are you going • to give me the twenty dances you promised me this morning? "he asked with a smile.

"No. certainly not," answered Bina laugh- ing. " Besides, I do not think I promised them when you asked for them, did I ? " • Ben shrugged .his shoulder g deprecatingly. "My mistake," he said with twinling eyes. 'But may I have the first waltz, to start with ? "

" I'm afraid it's promised." said Bina regretfully, holding out her programme, " to a maa who is staying with us." Ben Nevis was obviously disappointed, and a twinge of jealousy passed through his-mind. - " Well, at least, I may have the next ? " he asked, taking her card. She nodded‘and he dotted " 8.N." against four dances. "I've been very moderate," he said, hand- ing it back. "I've only taken the second, the sixth, the supper. dance, and one after ; so, perhaps, you will be able to spare me an extra later oa." - - -- - .

Bina could not help smiling at his audacity. " I do not know that I shall be able to keep all these," she :replied, with a touch of re- straint in her voice. " It's too many, you know." "Try." he whispered, making way for others who were waiting. • "If I have trans• greased the bounds of etiquette, you must ascribe it to my long absence from civilisation or to any other. adequate excuse you can think of I " _ .

„. . As he turned round he found himself face to face with Branksea, who was scowling por- tentously. But Ben Nevis forgave him from a kind of fellow-feeling. "In an hour or two I may feel like him,"• he said to himself, hardly daring to he opti- mistic, but determined to try his luck before the evening was out. Mr. Stuart meanwhile was standing under the wing of the Duchess of Hampstead, watch- ing the brilliant scene. Suddenly his hostess touched his arm. ” The King," she murmured. It was with mixed feelings that Otto Watched the entry of the royal party and noted the pleasant cordiality with which the King and the Queen greeted onc and another as they passed. "Surely they cannot be unpopular ? " he thought to himself. Previously this had struck him as the Weak .point of the scheme, but Fraser had explained it away. "Personally they are popular enough, but it is the price of food," he had said. "That is making the populace daily more discontented and ready for a change. They resent the 1.,-”TV of th,- ,wmer el " : " t - sance, 01 iitCli Lucy low. upon Joy ‘oay. as me head and the type. Do you imagine that it was simply the personal unpopularity of Louis XVI. and Marie Antoinette that brought about the French Revolution ? " The argument was unanswerable in itself ; but Otto felt that there would be many warm

" I saw I you driving him in your car in Piccadilty this afternoon.] • "Oh, did you ? " said Bina more sharply, realising not without a vague feeling of pleasure that he was a little jealous. "It was mother's suggestion. They treat him at home not only with the utmost graciousness, but even with a marked deference, which I do not understand. He seems to have sprung from nowhere or the skies, and I may tell you strictly in confidence that I believe he is some very big wig abroad, travelling ineoenito." Humph 1 " grunted Ben 'Nevis sus- piciously. "Anyhow, he seems familiar with all the other Eufopean courts and capitals; and," she ended up defiantly, "his manners are charming. Charlie has taken a tremendous fancy to him." 'He's no judge of character," commented Ben disparagingly. "He took to you at once," said Bina demurely. Ben Nevis laughed frankly, and Bina joined in. " You had me there fairly," he admitted, recovering his good humour. "You mustn't think me churlish, but I owe this mysterious Mr. Stuart a grudge for doing us out of Out morning's skating." , " 'Well, forgive him, now that it's all past," the girl suggested softly ; " and don't be cross with me ; it's not my fault that he is here or that he is nice. IC's a pleasant change to meet a than after some of these raw boys." " It is for you to forgive me," said Ben with contrition, pleased at the implied compliment. "I've been in a bad temper all day. Can't you guess why ? " "No," said Bina, growing suddenly in- terested in pulling an unoffending feather out of her fan, "unless the excitement of the week-end was too much for your shattered nerves." "Do be serious for a moment," pleaded Ben, leaning forward eagerly. "Here is Sir Alan Atherly coming to claim his dance," the girl said abruptly. "Just my luck," said Ben Nevis half audibly. • "I've kept the sixth dance safely for you," Whispered Bina coquettishly, as she greeted her new partner. Ben Nevis realised keenly for the next half hour what the sensations of Mahomet's coffin must have been, and his partners found him distrait and uninteresting, though he made spasmodic efforts to talk commonplaces. He watched Bina dancing the fifth dance with Branksea, and she smiled to him as she caught his eye in passing. This crumb of com- fort sustained the hungry lover and gave him fresh hope. As soon as decency permitted, with the open- ing bars of the next dance he claimed Bina from her partner, who seemed blacker and more ill - humoured than usual. Relations were obviously strained between them. Without a word the son of the house left Bina's side, greeting his rival with a hardly- suppressed scowl of disfavour. What have you done to put the amiable Branksea out of temper ? " asked Ben Nevis by way of greeting. "Oh, nothing," answered the girl in an annoyed voice, "only refusing for the second time the Marquisate of Swanage with its _attendant ills." "Poor Branksea," murmured Ben, 'masking his delight with feigned sympathy. "Shall we sit this out ? You seem tired." "I'm not tired," answered Bina laughing. "I'm cross. But, if you'll risk it, we'll stay where we are." They were comfortably 'screened behind some palms which showed that Bmnksea knew the geography of his own home. "I will risk it,' said Ben, scaling himself beside her on the settee, "and I want to risk something far more serious. Does it always make you cross to be proposed to?" "So far," monitored Bina, knowing that her time had come. "Well, I must risk your wrath," said Ben, speaking seriously, "or, dare I hope that you won't be angry with me ? " He paused for an instant as Bina made an impulsive movement. ' Dear," he went on, taking her hand with a boldness that surprised himself, "surely you must know how I love you ? Since I met you —only a few days ago, all told—it has made all the difference to my whole life, and I can't go on living without you. Can you—do you love me-? Tell me, Bina," he concluded, drawing her nearer to him. She did not resist, as she looked up with twimming eyes. - "I love you—l do love you ! " she said, with • the utmost simplicity and obvious ancerity. "And I could never have loved tnyone but you ! " 'Ben's heart bounded an though it would stop or burst, My darling —my heart's darling, at last 1 was all he could say; and he took her in his arms and kissed her on the lips.

div.head: £lO for the Most Amusing.
div.p: £lO for the Most Amusing.
[ALL ItIGIn-s ItbsiacrEi).) NATURE AND SPORT,
THE MARQUIS OF GRANBY (Author of " Trout Fishing," de.).

To which .section of those who pursue one or other of the representative sports of Great Britain—hunting, . shooting and fishing—is it given to be influenced most by the surroundings with which nature environs them while they fol- low their favourite amusement? lly this I mean, does the hunting man, when siding to the meet, appreciate the charm of the still, grey, November day? A day such as that described by Whyte Melville in the inimitable " Market Harborough "." the calm grey light of a mild winter's afternoon,"—or is his mind merely taken up by* the task of wondering whether he is going to have good or bad sport, and other kindred ideag ? Does the same iedi- sidual, when engaged in his favourite pursuit much later in the season,—say towards the end of. March, or the beginning of April,—derive any pleasure from the purple-green shoots in the fences, the pairing of the birds, the buds of the primrose, and the other thousand perfect promises of spring--(that is when anything in the nature of a seasonable, ordinary spring seems probable) ? or does he simply curse them all heartily, for so plainly letting him know that the time is rapidly approaching when he must cease from troubling the fox—for that season, at any rate? THE HUNTING MAN. 1 suspect that among all the classes of sports- men, the hunting man takes least inttrest in nature's signs—except as regards those which tend to show a forthcoming frost or thaw—; and that with but rare exceptions, for hunting men only the charms of the chase exist; Dame Nature's are too staid and prosaic for them. Of course I may be told that this is a gross libel, and that those who hunt are as devoted to the above mentioned lady as any. But if so it seems to me that the vast majority of them keep a stern bold over themselves, and do not permit their adoration to appear on the surface at all. Accepting. then, for the purpose of argument that the hunting fraternity do not seem to be as sympathetically inclined towards Nature's de- lights as it might be thought probable, what can we say as regards those who take their sporting pleasures in shooting? Do they study nature more than their hunt- ing brethren ? do they fall more under her sway? On the whole I should say "yes, they do." And very possibly this is so because of the difference of their environments. A man on the top of a high couraged, thoroughly "fit " horse, has, however good a horseman he may be, not very much spare time in which to study anything except those matters proceeding im- mediately around him ; that is, after he has reached the meet. On his way thither he may have noticed what was going on in the country- side, but when he lies arrived, his attention must of neceessity be taken up with many other af- fairs, and a long ride home in the dark at the end of the day, does not lend itself to a study of nature, except as to how best to prevent is tised horse from stumbling. NATURE AND THE GUN., How does this compare with the position in which a man finds himself during even the most prosaic day's covert shooting? Supposing the coverts to be the most formal and " tame " ones possible, nevertheless there is always plenty of wild bird life to be noticed, over and above the movements of the pheasants, bares and rabbits. While if shooting in mild weather at the end of January, as you probably may be when running through the coverts to thin off the wary cock pheasants, the promise of spring is to be then marked in the already formed greenish buds on honeysuckle binders and similar plants and shrubs; a stray, foolishly early primrose or two may even be found. while the indescribable, but unmistakable, feel of the coming spring is in the air, bidding you be of good cheer, and hopeful of fair times to come. At any period of the winter, moreover, the charms of nature are strongly in evidence, and, cannot be altogether Ignored by anyone who has eyes in his head to see and observe, though it be not his, or any- one else's, power to entirely comprehend their significance. What is more beautiful than the silvery work which is often spread by the Frost King over every inch of woods and hedges after a really cold sharp night? It may be vastly unpleasant for the beaters to have to force their way through coverts when they are thus clothed in white brilliance; but the cold charm of this fairy effect is unmistakable and wonderful. The most ordinary and uninteresting woods then have an unusual attraction. THE EYE-PLAY OF THE MOOES. Again, to turn our consideration towards another branch of shooting, namely, partridge driving, the quiet which ought to prevail during the period just before the drivs•s commence, at least as far as the sportsman himself is con- cerned, is very conducive to short studies of nature. For, while waiting, if the gunner and his loader will only remain still, keep their eyes open, and their senses alert, they may no- tice the habits and customs of many of the hedgerow inhabitants, such as tits, finches, and similar small birds, while they may glean some knowledge of the ways of the smaller four- footed beasts who also inhabit the fences. Surely the information thus gained all adds to the enjoyment of a day's shooting. Thus far we have only considered what pleasures can be ob- tained from observation and appreciation of nature when shooting amidst surroundings of the most ordinary, unromantic kind, in woods of the coin- monplace, flat-country sort, fields of the aver- age English type. Richard Jefferies has told us all, with a whole souled love of and devotion to nature and the English country which cannot easily be surpassed, how best to profit by 'atten- tive observation when living among country sights mid sounds. But obviously, to take as one example only, the level midlands of Eng- land are not as beautiful to the eye as the wild uplands of the west, the Derbyshire and York- shire moors and dales, or the stern delights of Scotland ; nor are they as fascinating as the wild heather and fir woods of some parts of the Eastern comities, or the beautiful valleys of Hampshire and Dorsetshire. In such places as these scenic impressions cannot fail to add large- ly to the charm of the day's shooting. So much has been written on this theme by men who were not only brilliant shots and most notable sportsmen—using the latter word in its best sense—but also writers of great power and charm—that it would be superfluous and indeed r presumptuous, to here do more than touch on ' the very fringe of the matter. 1 NATURE le EVERYWHERE. But a man must be very dense of soul, and altogether badly constructed who, when he is in battery on a moor on a warm clear August day, cannot feel the perfect charm which nature b:ts cre:thad Wl,At hnr amt trtelnr ha . On-

ated near one of the great manufacturing town:- of northern England, or whether it be one well over the border, in Scotland, matters leas than one would think. For the knowledge that the smoky 'ail which envelops a vast city, where steel and iron is worked, or that which hangs over a colliery district, is only just round the corner, so to speak, and is merely hidden from the sight of the sportsman by a protective bill. hardly lessens the delight of the mass of heather flowers, the faint rustle of the wonderful air through the patches of rushes and moor grasses, the joy of laying face downwards on the heather, and drinking in its sweet honey-fla- voured scent; while before the first grouse are seen moving in the far distance, the smaller moor birds, stone chats, whin chats, pipits, and the like, flit about, and afford endless interest to those who care to observe. It maybe, in- deed, that the scenery of English moors is not as grand and impressive as that of Scottish moors; though parts of Derbyshire and Yorkshire take much beating. But wherever heather is, there at once is a wonderful charm.

Again, can any one, when shooting over many parts of Norfolk and Suffolk, fail to be ',elf with the delights of the gorse, broom and heather-covered " heaths " of those counties ! See them on a brilliant October day, surrounded by apparently endless ?hie woods, glistening with fairy-like wreaths of dew spangles ; inhale the wondrous odours of the fir woods, and be very thankful. For the country wherein you are standing, is in its own way, possessed of great attractiveness, while none exceeds it in health-giving properties. Surely the delight of a good day's partridge driving is vastly enhanced by surroundings such as these f But little room is left to touch on the influ- ence of nature on fishermen. Possibly of all in these islands who follow some sport or other, none are brought so directly in touch with the influences which are communicated by rivers, wild flowers, birds, shrubs, and trees, let alone atmospheric conditions, •as are the followers of old haak's craft.

div.head: ANOl'.Eft.
div.p: THE ANOl'.Eft.

Anyone who really cares about fishing. whether it be for the lordly salmon or the more modest trout, or, to take one belonging to an- other branch of the angling fraternity, the bottom-fisher, cannot fail to notice—unless he be a miserable exception to what it...is_to be hoped is a very general rule—the delicacy of many of his surroundings, even though they be on the banks of one of the large " drains " so frequented by anglers in the Eastern counties. When trout fishing in early April in a West country or Derbyshire stream, cold though the weather may be,. nevertheless there are those tiny green shoots in the tree and shrub, among the rough grass on the river edges, mid on the banks, which promise those lovely wild flowers and grasses which are so delightful in that month, which the angler counts on for his Pis- catorial Paradise, namely June. If, in cold April, a gleam of sunshine is kind enough to appear, and to last for a quarter of an hour or so, is not there a fair probability of a sudden, almost magical. appearance of a rise of some early fly ?—dark olive Duns, or mayhap iron Blues? Should such a thing take place, the fisherman may rejoice ; for in all probability lie will be able to pick out a few trout during the rise, though from practical experience I sus- pect that he will not secure as many as the eagerness of the fish after the natural fly would presage ; spring rises, of iron blue duns especial- ly, being proverbially disappointing. But would anyone else, except a fisherman or a naturalist —and a fisherman should be both,—have noticed at all that Dame Nature was beginning her pro- lific work, amid the cold stern surroundings of early spring? I do not think many 'would have done so ; nor would they have marked, as it is to be hoped our fisherman did, the advent of some of those migrant birds who frequent our English rivers. The wagtail, the redstart— this latter not in early spring—the small sand- piper, the Chiff-chaff, and many another tiny visitor, who by plumage and by song bring added pleasures to a day's fishing.

div.head: TUE COMPENSATION OF ATIME.
div.p: TUE COMPENSATION OF ATIME.

Moving northwards to where the Scotch salmon rivers swing down from loch to sea, is there not always, at any time of the fishing year, even a more pronounced natural influence to be felt ? Do not the surroundings of the fisher- man go far to mitigate the miseries of a. blank day ? The wildness of the scenery, wherein he is engaged, or it maybe the more pastoral fea- tures of some of the lower reaches of certain salmon rivers, are constant in appealing to the angler with their varied beauties. The cry of the plover, the call of the grouse, the shy ap- pearance of the iingousel, the dive of the dip- per, the notes and curiosity-compelled com- panionship of many other moorland birds, such, as whinchats, stonechats, pipits, and the ever delightful wagtails, all tend to help a fisherman to enjoy to the full that sport of which be is so fond. Though his basket may be a light one, be will, if he be a true disciple of the craft, and therefore in sympathy with his environments, wend his homeward way with his heart in full accord with the gracious entertainment provided for him by nature.

So may it be with all real sportsmen, when. ever they take their pleasure in the country, whether or no that pleasure be in sports. May they never neglect to study—and thereby gain much profit—from the sights and sounds which nature places before all those who wisely look for them.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

The usual meeting of this Society was held on Sun- day last, ben Mr. T. L. Robins presided and referred to the recent eclipse of the sun, the predictions to the exact time. Showing the great wonders and power of the great God, who was also our Father. Mr. T. Lancaster of Manchester was the speaker, his subject being" Gather up the fragments that nothing be lost." There were fragments of opportunity,love and sympathy which was never lost. Mr. Miles and the Secretary also took part in the meeting. Mr. W. Pearse presided at the organ. Being a very wet thy, the attendance was not so good as usual. Two new members were heartily welcomed. Total now 523.

div.head: BAD TEETH AND DIGESTION.
div.p: BAD TEETH AND DIGESTION.
NOTTIEGIfAM MAN DESCRIBES ILi REGIS? terta'S INDIGESTION AND BILIOUSNESS BY NIOT SEIGEL'S SYRCP.

Of the many evils that besot modern life, few hive worse results than the early loss of teeth. "All my troubles arose from bad teeth," says Mr. Thomas Rawson, proprietor of the Prince Leopold Hotel, Moffatt-street, St. Anne's Well-road, Nottingham, in a letter to the proprietors of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, dated August 16th, 1905. " My teeth failed me verylearly in life," continues Mr. Rawson, "and I had the utmost dilliculty in chewing my food, being obliged to nibble like a rabbit, as one may say. "Of course, my digestive powers broke down under these unnatural conditions. At first pain and wind resulted from everything I ate, but it was not long before I was always in pain ; eating or fasting, I could not escape R. Often headache, accompanied by a drowsy feeling, which I was quite unable to overcome, completely unfitted me for work. Thus I continued, going from bad to worse, until at length my stomach became incapable of retaining any food at all ; it was rejected almost immediately it was swallowed. For some time I subsisted upon hot milk, being absolutely afraid to partake of anything more substantial. Poor diet for a man busily engaged all day 1 As I grew weaker, an additional trouble befel me—nothing less than rheumatism in my feet and legs—and my con- dition bacame that of a confirmed invalid. " For two years I was attended by a doctor ; but his utmost skill did no more than occasionally relieve me, and atthe end of that time I seemed as far from being cured as ever. It was the same with various patent medicines recommended to me, until I tried Mother Seigel's Syrup. Then my health began to mend. Soon I could relish and retain food, eating was not followed by pain, and rheumatism ceased to trouble me. At present my health is good, with every prospect of re- mainineso,fthough I still occasionally take a dose of the Syrup."

THE language of his COMPULSORY Majesty's present advisers SELF-APPROVAL, is never really intelligible except at those times, which are frequent, when they are praising them• selves or each other. The confidence which these gentlemen feel in themselves individually and in combination is something new to political life. The mood of what one of them has called" compulsory self-approval" is fixed and permanent. Mr. ARNOLD-FORSTER is a strongly illustrative case. He is a well-meaning, dogged, bat really rather feeble man. When he became War Minister the Army was in a bad way, for it had been in charge of Mr. BRODRICE. But under Mr. ARNOLD-FORSTER dis- order has become chaos. Disgusted officers have resigned in such numbers that it has been neces_ sary to find their successors among young men who have proved their inability to pass an examina- tion. It has even been necessary to advertise for officers who are to be passed into the Army with- out the usual preliminaries. There is the same difficulty in procuring men for the rank and file. We are no more prepared for war, Lord ROBERTS tells us, than we were previous to the long con— flict with the Boers. The Militia is in a condition of unserviceableness. The Volunteers have been so disgusted with their treatment that they are rapidly thinning away. And yet Mr. ARNOLD- FORSTER, who is responsible for this state of things, comes up smiling, complacent, self-confident. He actually believes, or professes to believe, that he has done a great work,which other men will be proud to carry on as his successors. He even nominates the Minister who is to succeed him. "I want Sir EDWARD GREY to carry on my work," he says, "and I believe he will." This is strange and even impudent language; but Mr. ARNOLD-FORSTER does not appear to have the least doubt as to its appropriateness, for if things are not right now, they are, it seems, to come right in three years time. We are then to have an Army " better found "than any British Army has ever been. The men are to be better men ; the Artillery is to be stronger; our armament generally is to be the best in Europe, and its organisation the best it has had for generations past. All this improvement is to be the consequence of a policy which has not even been adopted, and certainly cannot be carried out during the lifetime of the present Government. We do not know what leads Mr. ARNOLD-FonsTnn to fix upon Sir EDWARD GREY as his successor at the War Office. Perhaps it is the feeling that he can only be worthily succeeded by the ablest of the younger men on the Opposition Front Bench. But whoever does take up the task of reforming the War Office and reorganising the Army, when the present Government has been dispersed by a most

justly-wrathful people is not at all likely to begin where Mr. AnNoLn-FonsTEß:left off. He Will have to begin de new. That he will have produced results in three years' time:we do not doubt, any more !than that Mr. ARNOLD-FORSTER will endeavour to take credit for them. We shall pro- bably have him claiming the next Secretary for War as his pupil. It would seem almost as if Mr. BeLvotru had chosen his colleagues in considera- tion of their childlike belief in themselves, a characteristic from which,it must be said,he derives the principal part of his own distinction. Mr. ARNOLD-FORSTER ought by this time to 'be able to indulge in something more than prophecy in regard to the Army. He ought to be able to tell us what has been done and what is intended to be done. The Conservative party has been in power for more than ten years. Apart from the costs of war, it has expended on the Army sums of money enormously in excess of what has ever been ex- pended before. And what is the end of it all ?AA promise that we shall get an efficient and thoroughly organised Army under another Govern- ment in three years' time. Yet Mr.AuxoLD-FonsTER talks as if he were a great benefactor of the Empire!

Probably Captain UNIVERSAL TRAINING Crosfield will for- OR CONSCRIPTION. give us for saying that when we com- mented last week on Lord Esher's pronouncement against conscription we expected that he would be "drawn." There is nothing half-hearted about Captain Crosfield's enthusiasm for compulsory military training as a basis for national defence,and it was to be anticipated that he would not let the opportunity pass of challenging our views and advocating his own. The letter above his signa- ture, in our correspondence column, bears out our supposition. We have previously entered the lists with Captain Crosfield and had a friendly joust, not without profit, we hope, to our readers and all concerned. The subject, 'at the very least, merits thoughtful con- sideration and the fullest publicity. There is no doubt, unfortunately, that the state of our Army and its auxiliary forces is far from satisfac- tory. Inefficiency is widespread, and every remedial proposal, even one so extreme as that advocated by the National Service League, is entitled to respect. We are still no nearer to a basis of agreement with Captain Crosfield,however. His proposals involve an interference with the rights and freedom of the citizen, glib as the phrase may be, and we are not prepared to admit the slightest necessity for any such arbitrary measure. Compulsory training for only a few months does not seem very much to ask for on the face of it, but it is conscrip- tion in a mild form, and even Captain Crosfield appears to look upon conscription as an ugly word. But this is not the whole of the difficulty. We ask Captain Crosfield plainly if the adoption of the proposals of the National Service League would not place in the hands of the War Office a power which not only might, but in course of time very probably would, be abused? Is it not only too likely that the sweet simplicity of getting men by compulsion for periodical training would so appeal to the authorities that they would gradually enlarge the field of operations until we had a conscripted army? To us, such a sequel appears almost as inevitable as flood after rain. Universal training would solve the problem of national defence, but it is neither the sole nor the best means.

We entirely repudiate the charge of putting party before country," or seizing hold of "a good party cry," and we have yet to learn how, when, and where the question of universal training became a party cry. What party has espoused it, I I against whom is the cry upraised and for what ulterior object? Captain Crosfield has surely been incautious and hasty or he would never have made such an allusion. We quite appreciate the !value of a good party cry in political warfare, but this is not political warfare. It is a question which concerns every young man in the country alike,and involves the sacrifice of a great principle, that of national and individual freedom. We put principle before party, and freedom even before national defence or military glorification.

Whilst it is undeniable that HOPE FOR THE the competition of schemes for UNEMPLOYED. the solution of the unemployed problem is a healthy sign of the times, it is just possible that the theoretical philan- thropists are losing sight of the urgency of the situation. The icy blast of winter has already blown into fireless homes. The pinch of poverty, which always hurts most under a cold sky, is being felt with irresistible acuteness. Under such circumstances the time consumed in -discussion of methods of relief should be cut down to an irreducible minimum. It is clear that the emigration projects are bound to be hung up for some time, The proposals to send the submerged tenth "back to the manless land " appear to have yielded no other reeult than a weird kind of philan- thropic jealousy. Meanwhile, the problem clamours for solution. There are those who hope that the direct appeal to the King will bring relief. At all events' it is certain that the It iyal sympathy with the poor, the desolate, and the oppressed will stimulate the authorities in their efforts to grapple with the question. The demand for a special session of Parliament to provide for the anticipated danger is by no means irrational ; but should the consequences of the reception of the workers' petitions by his Majesty be those which may reasonably be expected, the necessity for such an unusual course of action will be re- moved. The auguries all point to a national deter- mination to settle this burning question once for all ; and the nation's will is law.

In this Nelson year :NELSON AND LovE. muc h has been written about his affection for Lady Hamilton' and opinion oscillates between the extremes of Lord Rosebery, who speaks of her a baneful influence," and her latest biographer and apologist. Nelson in his loves was, like many another sailor, prodigal. When he was twenty-four, and in command of the Albemarle frigate be visited Quebec, and there fell in love with a lady of that city. He was prevented from offering her his hand by the interference of his friend Alexander Davidson—" perhaps," as Southey tells us, "in an evil hour for himself." Two other passions he indulged before be met Mrs. Nisbet, the day of his marriage to whom he describe I shortly after the battle of the Nile as the happiest in his life. Lady Nelson has been blamed as often as her famous husband for the domestic infelicity which came to them after he had fallen under the influenee of "dear Lady Hamilton." She was not a hero's wife, as her letter to him urging him after the battle of St. Vincent, not to undertake the danger- ous work of boarding the enemy's ships himself, but to " leave it for captains," shows. But Captain Mahan tells us of her sad remark to her little grandchild: "When you are a little older, little Fan, you may know what it is to have a broken heart !"—an evidence that she felt more keenly his desertion than might be judged from other incidents. It is the custom to contrast Lady Nelson's mild manner and timidity for her husband's safety with the spirit which is alleged to have drawn from Nelson the exclamation : "If there were more Emmas there would be more Isl3lsons" ; but it is only fair to remember that the story of which this remark is part rests merely on the authority of Lady Hamilton herself.

The correspondence columns JAPANESE of several newspapers have been IMPERFECTIONS. used much of late with the idea of correcting popular English impressions of the Japanese. A Bishop, who has both a regard for our allies and respect for their conspicuous virtues, has warned Englishwomen agair,st hasty marriage contracts with members of the other race. Another observation by him,that, in

business affairs, the Japanese have not the high probity which their patriotism would suggest, has been met by some remarkable evidence as to their honesty. The domestic conditions, and especially the Japanese conception of what is due to . mother.in.law, should make the English girl pause, and do so without disrespect. As to the other matter, it is difficult to judge. Sharp deal- ing in commerce has increased in our own country in recent years; but honesty is still for the most part our policy. The shady transactions make a show out of proportion; and we may hope that this is true also of the Japs. The most serious consideration, one that will cause our working ' classes anxiety as it is realised, is the comparative indifference of the Eastern nations to the regula- tion of labour.. Tnis is not a mere question of pay. ,It is one of length of hours and sordid circum- stances. The manufactories of the towns are apt Ito make our own operatives reflect. We may hope that contact with the West will lead to an im- provement ; but the desire for markets, and to cut out importations by cheapness, are tempting. Therein lies the Yellow Peril—if there be one.

The work of wideninc, Sa-nkey Street is progressing. From Legh street to Bank House the thoroughfare will soon be of ample width. When the whole of Sankey street has been similarly improved, Warrington will ha--e reason to be proud of this—one of its main arteriee. * * * It may not be generally known that the late Sir Henry Irving,whose loss the nation sincerely deplores, visited Warrington many years ago.
