The hubbub eaused by kr. E. Plinston's somewhat mixed profession of political faith has resulted in his retirement from the candidature of Bewsey Ward. His place in the field has been already taken by Mr- James Dickenson who stands as aa Independent candidate. _ _

Yuch to the relief of Mr:. John D. Rockefeller, the richest man in the world, whom experience has taught to expect that he must form the topic of some scathing pulpit reference every Sunday, American preachers are now largely occupying themselves in denouncing the American insurance scandals. * * * " Darkston Ash is another grim pothook in the moral death-sentence which is terrifying Belshazzar Balfour. We are tired of exulting over Liberal triumphs. Our Frans are exhausted. Our transports are out of stock. We can find no new adjectives to express our delight. We are inured to victory and hardened to conquest."—" The Star."

* * "A soft answer turiaeth away wrath." Canon Morley Stevenson has a diplomatic way of dealing with objections raised during the School Dlanagement procedure,and on Monday by a voluntary explanation ho succeeded in avoiding what would probably have been a heated and personal discussion. It would be well if more public men were given to this tactful way of mollifying aggrieved questioners.
I

* The use of metaphors by public speakers is oft- times dangerous. For instance a Cymric orator at a recent meeting in Wales was holding forth, amid cot- tinuous interruptions,on the vexed education question. He exclaimed warmly, "here we are, up to our necks in the mire ! " (Interruption). The Chairman (appealingly) : " Sit down, gentlemen! Sit down, I ask you once again ; yes, indeed ! " * * * If a stranger in Dublin asks a jarvey what the street names, newly printed in the Irish language the latest Nationalist fad—mean, the driver replies " Musha, I don't know ; they're too lamed for me," The tobacconists were some of the first who took uP the fad. One was getting his name painted up, and a passing carman stopped to look at it ; then he said to his fare ; " D--those Hebrews, they are every- where !"

* * * Conditions of life in Germany, we imagine, will not be much longer extolled by Protectionists. The " Munich Post" publishes the following announce- ment : " All the meat exposed on the Freibank (where diseased meat, after being boiled, is retailed cheaply to the very poor) this, Wednesday morning, was bought up before ten o'clock." The price of horseflesh, we are told,has risen, and dog's-flesh is no longer obtainable.

* * * It ts one hundred years to-day (Saturday), since Lord Nelson defeated the combined fleets Of France and Spain, and received a fatal shot while directing operations from his flagship "The Victory." The Navy League suggest that the day should be celebrated in honour of Nelson by the hoisting of flags and ia any other manner which might be found practicable- This suggestion is supported locally by a circular letter from the Mayor. Get out your bunting, Y° patriots I. * * The immortal Bumble has told us that "the law io a hass,"but a certain Lepton "bass "is not enamoured ,of the law. Quietly rambling on the highway the ' other day, the donkey was espied by a police officer who forthwith attempted to take it into custody. The animal, however, happens to be well versed in the art ' of retaliation and tore the policeman's trousers and kicked out in all directions. Now, however, its fighting propensities will probably be checked as the owner has been fined. * * * Among the many good stories lan MacLaren (D John Watson) tells, is the following :—A gentleman. from the land of the star-spangled banner followea him to Liverpool, tracked him to his house, sent UV his card, and immediately followed it into the author'e study. "My name is Elijah K. Higgins," he breath- lessly exclaimed, "and I am a busy man; you also are a busy man, and have no time to 'fool away. Four days are all I can give to your United Kingdom, and I wished to shake hands with you. Good-bye. roa off to Drumtochty." And he vanished. * * Even Mr. Marshall Hall, K.C., the Conservative member for Southport, is not inclined to swallovr holus bolus everything the Government does, and ill a speech the other evening he fell foul of the Secretar9 for War, Mr. H. 0. Arnold-Foster. After expressing the opinion that we ought to have the volunteere brought up to the greatest possible state of efficiencY he said : " Mr. Arnold-Foster was a man of enor- mous ability, but he was not practical. He sva9 theoretical, he was nervous, and in his, Mr. Ilalrs, opinion he had no manners. He chose to ride rough- shod over everybody, and though no doubt in theorY he was an able man he was not the man to he at the head of the War Office." Nevertheless we are PaYi.ng Mr. Arnold-Foster £5,000 a year for making confusion worse confounded.

* * * Despite several months of discussions and deputn'l tions the physical instruction of school children etia remains a vexed question in Warrington. Now thalr the Education Committee and the Gymnasium Coni; mittee have settled their dispute the head teachers cu. the town as well as the managers of the Warrington British School are up in arms against the new arrange-- ments. The teachers object to the importation of out. side supervision which they say is not necessary 2 bgs probably they will be satisfied with Canon MN". Stevenson's explanation that the inspector's visit 41 not be of an inqnisatorial nature but merely with the object of giving friendly advice. Anyhow the schefl'? has received the sanction of the authority and eItPIL, ence will prove the wisdom or othezwise of the parture.

Anniversary Services at Latchford. The anniversary services in connection with Latch- ford Baptist Church were held on Sunday, the preacher being the Rev. J. F. Matthews. Despite the heavy rain, the morning service was well attended. In the afternoon the cantata "Promises of Jesus" was ably rendered by the choir there being a crowded congrega- tion. Mr. Harrison presided at the organ. Again in the evening the building was crowded. The preacher took for his text the words "Thou hast left thy first love." The offertories for the day amounted to H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE Tosco takes away that tired feeling.—(Advt.) Smoking Concert. The members of the Cemetery Hotel Bowling Club spent an enjoyable evening on Thursday, when a smoking concert was held at the headquarters. An excellent tea was provided after which the evening was pleasantly spent in speech-making and song. The popular president of the club, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, was in the chair, and his health was heartily drunk on the proposition of Mr. E. A. Boardman. The health of the vice presidents was also suitably honoured. Songs were rendered by Messrs. J. Allison, J. E. Harrison, Ball, W. J. Whittle, S. Green, J. Harrison and W. J. Ball. The prizes won in connection with the closing main were distributed by Mr. A. H. Crosfield as follows : A. J. Jones, 1 ; R. Rothwell, 2 ; A. Scott, 3; S. Ratcliffe, Ball, T. Humphreys, J. F. Whittle, J. Haslem, J. Berry, W. Jones, John Monks, R. Antrobus, and C. Newton. Consolation prizes, W. Butterworth, •F. Millar, T. Jones, W. Swanton, J. Bramhall, George Monks, W. Hill and P. Podmore. UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS.—Advt.

Ancient Order of Foresters, Warrington District. The officers and brethren paid their last tribute of respect to the late P.C.R. Bro. James Marsh, of Rolles- tog-street, Warrington, on Saturday. A procession was formed from the house, and they walked to the Cemetery. Amongst the various representatives were :—D.C.R. Bro Hipkiss, S.D.C.R. Bro. Councillor P. Peacock, P.D.C.R. Bro. Davies, District Secretary, P.D.C.R. Bros. Chrimes, James, Hankinson, Brown ; also Trustees Bros. Walsh, Gregory and Smith.—The annual District Meeting was postponed until after the ceremony, and the delegates and officers proceeded by 'bus to the Horse and Jockey, Martinscroft. The Secretary (Bro. Davies) gave particulars of substan- tial increase in funds, and reported a membership in 1 Warrington District of over 1,600. The election of officers took place, and the S.D.C.R. Bro. Councillor Peter Peacock was installed as District Chief 1 Ranger, and Bro. Joseph Owen as Deputy. The meet- ing was adjourned for tea, and after a substantial repast, the business was proceeded with, and the dele- gates assembled took the opportunity of reviving the suggestion of not only haring_ representative on the Education Committees, but on Boards of Guardians, also Town Councils.—After an enthusiastic discussion ' by P.D.C.R. Bro Chrimes, Bullock, Hipkiss, and H. • • Maybury, and Trustees Bros. Walsh and Smith, it was unanimously resolved to ask all Warrington Foresters . to support Chief Ranger Bro. Councillor Peter Peacock for election in Bewsey Ward on November Ist, and to ask Federated Friendly Societies to assist him as 'their nominee.—Councillor Peacock thanked them for the complimentary remarks, and gave a brief account of his work in the Council, and particularly as to how ' Friendly Societies gained by having sympathetic repre- sentatives there. div.head: FATAL AFFRAY AT SANKEY.
div.p: FATAL AFFRAY AT SANKEY.
FOUR MEN IN CUSTODY.
Proceedings at To-day's Inquest.

IA quarrel attended by fatal consequences occurred jat Sankey on Sunday night last. A number of Irish farm labourers were in the Butchers' Arms when high • words ensued and the men, amongst whom was John Flemming, were ordered off the premises. On Monday Flemming complained to the police of having been brutally kicked, and was removed to the Workhouse Infirmary where he died later in the day. In house- I quenoe of the statements which he made four men Patrick Noone, Thomas Conniff, John Lattrn and Michael Garrity were arrested. The Coroner's inquiry was conducted at the Warring ton Police Station, this (Friday) morning by Mr. S. Brighouse. Mr. A. Browne attended on behalf of the -prisoners, and Superintendent Strickland on behalf of the police. Mr. Brighouse said the proceedings would not take so long as he anticipated as the police were desirous that in the interests of justice j the inquest should he adjourned to enable them to make further inquiries which would place I them in a position to give the case more completely I and fully than they could do that morning. After re-capitulating the circumstances of the case Mr. Brighouse said that the post-mortem examination placed , beyond doubt the fact that the man's death was due to ! injuries received. Late on Monday night what were J supposed to be Flemming's dying depositions were *ken but Mr. Browne would no doubt have something I to say as to whether those depositions were admissable I or not. .

Thomas Flemming, farm labourer, gave evidence of identification. His brother, who was 25 years of ago, was a labourer on Lindley Green Farm, Sankey. Mr. Browne asked that he might be supplied with a copy of Flemming's depositions. Mr. Brighouse said he would supply Mr. Browne with a copy as he desired him to give some assistance at the adjourned inquest to decide whether they were adsnissable.The four prisoners were charged with doing grevious bodily harm to Flemming at 7.10 p.m. on Monday. At 10.20 p.m. the same day Flemming's depositions were taken. The law said that the magis- trate who took the depositions should add thereto byway of caution, the reasons why they were taken. In that case it had not been done,and,further,no notice had been given to the persona in custody that the de- positions were to be taken so that they might have the opportunity of cross-examining Fleming as to the state- ments he made. _ _
The iiipTe-si-I'vas adjourned until next Friday. POLICE COURT PROCEEDINGS.

The proceedings at the Occasional Court on Tuesday, when the prisoners were charged with the wilful murder of Flemming, were-Lot a purely formal character, only evidence of arrest being given. When taken into custody the men were charged with infiictinz grievous bodily harm upon the man Flemming at Sankey, by kicking him, breaking his jaw, and causing internal injuries. Noone replied that he was at the Chapel House,on Sunday night and left at Bo'clockgoing straight home with Cunniffe. He went to bed at 9 p.m. Cunniffe said he went home with Noone, two men from Mr. Taylor's being with them. Laheen said he was at the Butcher's Arms until 9.40, and did not see Flemming up or down. Garrity said he came along with him (probably Laheen) and he did not see the bother. After the death of Flemming the men were charged with wilful murder. Cunniffe and Laheen made no reply. Noone replied: "Me And Jack (meaning Laheen), never saw him after became out of the public- house." Garrity said: "I never touched Jack Flemming; I got hit in the bother, and told the boss I could not turn out this morning, my eye being swelled up-"

In defending a publican against a prosecution for permitting gaming. Mr. S. Brighouse said it was an offence to play any game on licensed premises even for a three-halfpenny "gill." If defendant wanted to gamble for drinks he could, said the solicitor-coroner, "go to Onnskirk Parish Church bazaar next month. and for sixpence could have, in a lottery, a chance of winning a bottle of brandy under the auspices of the clergy." This is as blunt as the coroner knows how to make it. We should think this bazaar would be a good opportunity. for the enterprising policeman. Lotteries are " agin the law," Even when sponsored by the clergy.

on each and every occasion. The love duet with Nanki- Poo " Were you not to Ko-Ko plighted" is one of the most" taking" passages in the opera, and here again interest in Mrs. Booths efforts often reset() enthusiasm. Successful Performances by Members Mrs Garton Stone is to be complimented on a success- ful 'debut. Although having had only a cornpara- of the Musical S • ociety. tively short time in which to perfect herself in the part of Pitti-Sing, she has entered into the spirit of it with zest,and has combined a sweetness of vocalisation with an engagingly vivacious manner. Her one great opportunity occurs in the singing of For he's going to marry Yum-Yum "and in the bit of cajolery by which she tries to make the stern Lord High Everything Else unbend, in all of which it is due to say she acquitted her- self most satisfactorily. Miss Marie Houghton also makes very promising first appearance. Her work as Peep-po is,of course of minor importance, but it may at once be said that she has made the most of it and in association with her two sisters helped to make up a prettily effective group. A gem of harmony is the well-known madrigal Brightly dawns our wedding day." The voices of Yurn-Yum, Nanki-Poo, and Pish- Tush, here blend with very pleasing effect and the whole of the parts being given with brightness and precision, the number has elicited many encores. The five-part glee " See how the fates their gifts allot " is an equally enjoyable number, and given by Pitti-Sing, Katisha, The Mikado, Ko-ko and Pooh-Bah, its piquant performance has at all times been pleasurably greeted to the audience. One of the most striking successes of the opera has been achieved by Miss Nellie Anderton in the part of Katisha. It is evident that she has made a very careful study of a somewhat unin- viting part, into which she throws herself with a dramatic forcefulness which is as admirable as it is fall of promise. This is particularly noticeable when she breaks in upon the revels of the multitude in the very picturesque finale to the first actin vehement endeavours to disclose the identity of Nanki-Poo. It is only in Katisha's music that the element of pathos is felt. Miss Anderton's rendering therefore of such passages as " The hour of gladness is dead and gone " and the song "0 living I " is characterised by a full-toned contralto voice, used with good taste and excellent effect. The chorus is both highly efficient and well balanced in its various gections, and has capably supplemented the work of the principals. The separate choruses for the men and the ladies occurring at the opening of the opera are sung with refreshing crispness, brisk action contributing to numerous loictureque situations. Especially pretty is the entry of the ladies as they sing " Comes a trail' of little ladies " with its charming two-part melodies and dainty orchestral accom- paniment. The ensemble effects have from a spectacular as from a musical point of view been finely realised, the conclusion of Act I. with its busy movement and the inter-play of principals and chorus, being especially worthy of high praise,the re-demand for the disclosing of the stage-picture veiled by the falling curtain, being in itself a kigh compliment to all con- cerned. A very complete and competent orchestra, under the able leadership of Mr. R. H. Pearson, has contributed very materially to the all-round success of the opera. Mr. Frank H. Crossley again skilfully wields the baton and as musical director is to be credited with I raore than a moiety of the opera's successful run. No one will be more gratified with the suceess of"Tbe Mikado" than Mr. B. Thornley Dodge. He has thrown I himself into the duties of stage manager with an earnestness and a determination to leave nothing to chance which earns its reward in so successful a sequel. ' The arrangements for the opera have been in the hands of a hard-working committee consistingof Messrs. J. W. Bibby, H. Bond, F. H. Crossley and J. Newcombe (hon. secretary and treasurer.) The scenery, properties and limelight were supplied by Le Maistre and Co., Man- chester, the costumes and appurtenances by 13urkinshaw and Sons, Liverpool, and the wigs and" make-op "by Birch Browne and Son, Warrington.

It was with the confidence inspired by previous triumphs that the members of the Warrington Musical Society embarked upon their third amateur operatic enterprise, and the performances of " The Mikado " which have been given in the Parr Hall each evening this week bid fair to add another laurel to the com- pany's record. Such a success is in itself no small tribute to the entertaining capalfilities of the perform- ers, for the productions of " The Yeomen of the Guard" and" The Gondoliers" had set a standard which it is highly creditable to see is fully main- tained in the presentment of "The Mikado." The Musical Society is to be congratulated upon having in in its ranks members who have figured so worthily in a realm quite unfamiliar to them until the venture of of three years ago. It is hardly necessary to remind our readers of the gratifying outcome of the opera enterprises. The proceeds have been sufficient to extinguish a large debt and place the Society in a sound position to continue its useful work. But apart from the commendable nature of the object, the new departure has been welcomed by a very large section of the townspeople as affording them opportunities of enjoying some of the choicest of the Gilbert-Sullivan collaborations. The large and enthusiastic audiences at the Parr Hall this week have testified in a marked degree to the popular apprecia- tion of these works and we feel sure that, in express- ing the hope that "The Mikado" will be only one of a long series of similar successful presentments of light opera, we are voicing the wishes of the majority of Warringtonians. The choice of " The Mikado " was in all respects a happy one. For the time being, the stage presents a scene of rich Oriental splendour, and the opera itself sparkles with gaiety and humour. The words reflect Gilbert in his merriest vein, while the music is of that vivacious and tuneful character which charms the ear from beginning to end. Of course, such a work demands brightness and abandon on the part of most of the artistes, and the Warrington amateurs have in this way attained most satisfactorily what is often a difficult essential. There is rollicking fun on the stage , engendering, of course, unrestrained mirth in the hall, and for tbe time being " dull care "is banished. The " plot "—if one might apply the term to comic opera —centres round the love affairs of Nanki-Poo, (the son of the Mikado who astounds his royal father by dis- appearing from the imperial Court and masquerading as a strolling musician), and Yum-Yum, one of the attractive wards of Ko-Ko, the Lord High Executioner of Titipu. When it is known that at the opening of the story Yum-Yum is betrothed—unwillingly,of course,— to her exalted guardian, while Nanki-Poo is being per- secuted with the attentions of Katisha' an elderly and by no means attractive personage who is determined to become %is wife, the possibilities of complications and ludicrous situations are apparent. Of course, when the skein has become sufficiently entangled it is just as ingeniously unravelled, and everything ends as it should do. The cast is a small ono, thus involving a great reSponsibility on the part of the principals, but the manner in which those entrusted with the leading ',les have acquitted themselves is worthy of all praise. From the moment when the uprising curtain discloses the picturesque court-yard of Ko-Ko's official residence to the picturesque finale in the last act, the sprightly songs and dances and merry quips and cranks hold the unflagging interest of the audience. And here it may be said that it is by no means easy to recognize even one's intimate acquaintances when made resplendent in gorgeous Eastern costumes and beautified by a Japanese make-up." Each evening the audiences have been considerably puzzled in making out the personality of the cliorus,n.otably at the beginning of the first act when a group of Japanese nobles are seen disporting themselves in the quaint yet picturesque attitudes. The reappearance of most of the principals who have gained laurels in previous operas has been a source of gratification to the public, while several new-comers have completely justified their inclusion and met with very cordial receptions. One favourite in the person of Mr. ,J. Babbitt, as Nanki-Poo, makes an fine entry a few minutes after the raising of the curtain. His part this year is not quite so exacting as that which he has been called upon to play in former years, nevertheless it affords him plenty of scope for the display of his histrionic and musical abilities. He fulfils the role exceedingly well, infusing just the requisite dramatic touches into his passionate declara- tion of love for Yum-Yum and his determination to commit the "happy dispatch " if he is not allowed to marry her. It is, however, in the coral numbers that Mr. Babbitt excels, his pure-toned tenor voice enabling him to finely interepret the opening song" A wandering minstrel I " with its spirited choruses, for i which he s nightly encored. Having made Pknown to the gay assembly that he has come to seek Yum-Y urn, the love-bra minstrel soon has the benefit of the in- teresting though not very encouraging information regarding his prospects which is imparted by Pish-Tush, a noble lord, impersonated by Mr. W. H. Wallington. A remarkable functionary, who makes an early appear- ance on the scene, is Pooh-Bah, whose multifarious offices, ranging from First Lord of the Treasury to Lord Mayor of Titipu, are summed up in the title "Lord High Everything Else." Mr. J. W. Bibby takes this port most admirably. He is dignity and exclusiveness per- sonified, as bats one who is proud to trace his ancestry back to "a protoplasmal primordial atomic globule." Nothing—not even the blandish- ments of the coquettish little maids—can induce him to relax his austerity. Reaching the height of con&scen- sion when'ihe says "How-de-do, little girls ! " to the fair visitors, it goes sorelyagainst the grain to have to do humble obeisance in the presence of the Mikado later in the work. Mr. Bibby's rendering of the part is the more acceptable to the audience because his pro- nuniciation is so c•onderfiilly distinct,and he sings with fine effect his chief song " Yonng man, despair," which, with its animated chorus, has proved immensely popular during the week. Quite a profusion of ceremony heralds the advent of Ko-Ko, the Lord High Executioner. The full chorus takes up the martial strain " Behold the Lord High Executioner," the retinue entering with due stateliness, and as the great man him- self appears, armed with his huge official sword, all prostrate themselves before him. As Ko-Ko Mr. C. P. Gough has scored a signal triumph. The personality of Ko-Ko dominates the entire opera, and there is no denbt that in his impersonation of this character Mr. Gough has deserved, as he has attainecl,premier honours. It was early seen that Mr. Gough had realized its possi- bilities to the full, his grotesque antics keeping the house in continual merriment. Mr. Gough is undoubt- edly seen at his best in the second act when, suing for the love of Katisha, he touches her heart by singing that lugubrious ditty " On a tree by a river a little tom-tit." Another very catching song of tio-Ko's is the one occurring earlier "I've got a little list" with its candid enumerations of the persons who "never would be missed " if they were disposed of by a bene- ficent public executioner. The duet The flowers that bloom in the Spring," by Nanki-Poo and Ko-Ko is one lof the most mirth-provoking numbers. Ko-Ko has just' been told that there is no alternative but for him to marry the unattractive Katisha, and throughout the sprightly duet he wears the most doleful expression, ending by singing an encore verse in mock tears. The item has thoroughly delighted the audiences and has been encored time after time each evening. Mention must be made of the somewhat unique trio "I am so proud" in which Ko-Ko, Pooh-Bah, and Pish-Tush seek to give ponvincing reasons why one of them should not be executed to avert irretrievable ruin to Titipu and its men of rank. This is really the most difficult number , in the score, and though its performance has never " taken on' with the audience to the extent of eliciting much applause, there has been both conscien- tious and painstaking work shown in its inter- pretation. The thrilling and weird story of the execution recounted to the Mikado and Katisha by the conspirators Ko-Ko, Pitti-Sing and Pooh-Bah bulks largely each evening as a mirth provoking scene, the honours of which it would be invidious to divide other than equally amongst these three. In the title role Mr. Pred Fieldhonse does not make his appearance until well on in the second act. His arrival is however attended with such great pomp as to create quite a diversion, provi- ding another pleasing spectacular display. On the whole Mr. Fieldhouse comports himself in a manner well befitting the part and in the well known song "My object all sublime ' he nightly earns his quota of the i ' audience's plaudits. The four ladies included in the cast each sustains her part with the distinction and credit proportionate to its importance. It is with the appearance of the "Three Little Maids" that the gaiety begins in earnest. The parts are entrusted to Mrs. Arthur Booth (Yum-Yuni), Mrs. C. Garton Stone (Pitti-Sing) and Miss Marie Houghton I (Peep-bo) all of whom introduce themselves in the delightful trio "Three little maids from school are we." Needless to say, Mrs. Booth's past operatic achieve- meets bespoke for her a hearty reception by the public, forming also a guaraLtee that she would further dis- tinguish herself. Nor were expectations falsified, the highly capable manner in which she has acquitted herself in the central character of the • charming "Yum-Yum " being a theme of general admiration. There is a freedom from restraint and act arming d's- ingenuousness about her acting, that made success at once possible, her impersonation of Yurn-Yum being backed up by expressive and artistic renderings of the music attached to the part. Mrs. Booth possesses a fine soprano voice of still increasing flexibility, and each evening she has greatly pleased the assembly with her rendering ot the beautiful song" The sun whose rays are all ablaze"in the second act,repetitions being demanded

div.p: "THE MIKADO."
FIRE BRIGADE TOURNAMENT. Novel Competitions at Messrs. Crosfield's Works.

Warrington people had on Saturday afternoon an opportunity of witnessing some of the most up-to-date methods of tire-fighting. The occasion was the annual tournament in connection with Messrs. Joseph Cros- field and Sons, Warrington and Liverpool fire brigades and, notwithstanding the bitterly cold weather, the event attracted a large assembly to the works yard at Bank Quay. Amongst those present were : MLA. H. Crosfleld, Captain G. R. Crosfield, Dr. Markel, Mr. F. J. Lord, Mr. H. Kingdon, Councillors Ashcroft, Burton, Barton, Wright, A. Peacock, Mr. Frank Turner, jag., (deputy superintendent of the Warrington Fire Brigade), Mr. Parker (superintendent of the Winwick Asylum Fire Brigade), Captain Shaw (superintendent of the Salford Fire Brigade), Mr. Fox (Crosfleld's Fire Brigade Liverpool), and Mr. Newall (chief engineer of Messrs. Crosfleld and Sons). The major part of an exceptionally interesting programme was provided by the Warrington brigade whose efficiency is a matter for congratulation. The various tests were gone through very smartly and gave one the impression that the men should be able to cope with any outbreak if occasion arises. In the compc,titien with the Liverpool team however, the Warrington men had to admit defeat. Six men, one of whom acted as Superinten- dent, had to answer an alarm, run out 180 feet of hose from the hydrant, and fix the branch pipaand standpipe in position. Both squads gave a good display, but the Liverpool men were considerably the smarter. Allow- ing for penalties they did the work in 22 2-5 secs,,while the Warrington men took 27secs, Another drill takenl part in by the Warrington men alone illustrated how a tire at the works could be coped with if only eight men answered an alarm, while in another exacting test the brigade had to accomplish a change of front,due to a; second- call immediately following the first. To the , average spectator the life saving display and full turnl out were the most interesting features. There were several gallant rescues by different methods from a warehouse which was supposed to be ablaze, the brigade manipulating the escapes with great promptitude. The full turn out was quite exciting. On the alarm being given a small hand-drawn 300 gallon Shand-Mason steamer was brought into play in 50secs., followed shortly afterwards by a large 800 gallon Shand engine. The hoses were soon fixed and great jets of water shot into the air, tho use of "spreaders " being interestingly illustrated. The display concluded by the throwing of a powerful stream of water to the height of 190 feet. The judges were Captain Shaw, of the National Fire Brigade Union ; Captain Parker, of Winwick Asylum Brigade ; and Captain Gallon, of Messrs. Crosfleld's Brigade. The following were the winners and their times : Dressing Drill : 1, Whitby, 23 4-ssec. ; 2, Beaman, 25 4-ssecs. ; 3, Holden, 29 1-ssecs. ; 4, Warbur- ton, 27 1-ssec.: 3, Cooke, 35sec. Hose cart drill : 1, Whitby's squadron (eight men) 31 I-ssec. ; 2, Webh's squadron, 42 1-ssec.; 3 Herchell's squadron, 43sec. ; Holden's squadron, 46sec. ; Southern's squadron, 50sec. Steamer event : 1, Whitby's squadron, Ist call 30sec., 2ni call 63 1-ssec., total 93 1-ssec.; 2, Herchell's squadron. Ist call 27 2-s,iec., 2nd call -67 sen., total 91 2-ssec.; 3, Webb's squadron, Ist call, 30sec., 2nd call 65 4-ssec., total 95 4-ssec. ; Holden's squadron, Ist call 39 2-ssec., 2nd call 62sec., total 101 2-ssec.; Southern's squadron, Ist call 35sec., 2nd call 91 1-ssec., total 126 1-ssec. Liverpool v. Warrington event :, Liverpool, ' 22 2-7. see. ; Warriugton, 27sec. The winning team were penalized 2sec., and Warrington isec. During the after- noon enjoyable selections of music were given by the works band. At the close, the prizes were distributed by Captain CROSF [ELM who congratulated the men upon the excel- lent competitions that had been witnessed. There was, he said, a danger of apathy creeping into even fire brigade matters when the call to arms never came and they never got a chance of putting their theory into practice, or, if he might so term it in their case, put their practice into practice. The great value of the ' competions was that they kept the men keenly alive,and ' they served to show the efficiency or otherwise of the corps. In these days of sloping shoulders and slouching gait, it was very pleasant to look upon men so well set as the members of the brigade, and he could to some extent realize the trouble and the self-sacrifice which they had been put to to arrive at that state of physical alertness, and that disciplined attitude of mind which was so essential to success. But he would have them remember that in those works, they were only satisfied with "the best possible "and the brigade had a long way to go yet before they arrived at that. They should remember that true heroism consisted in persist- ency, and they should continue to persist until they had brought the National Shield from the Crystal Palace, and brought honour and glory to themselves and to the firm. (Applause). The teams and a number of guests were entertained to tea in the Assembly Room.

Progressive Labour League. A meeting of this League was held on Tuesda) evening, Mr. Thomas Barnes presiding over an excep- tionally good attendance. A syllabus for the session was arranged and the November elections were dis- cussed. At the meeting on Tuesday next the subject for discussion will be " Back to the land."

On Monday Warrington turned out the same side to do battle with Bradford, and there was quite a trans- formation. Every man was at his best and the com- bination between halves and threequarters was brilliant. Knight quite redeemed himself and did some magnificent kicking, while Brooks and Hocken- hall at half-back gave quite their best display, On Monday's form there would be no need to look further for the right kind of half-back. It generally results in them getting the ball, and possession is the first part of the verb "to score." A team with a weak back division has some excuse for taking a man from the pack at critical moments, but in Warrington's case it is rank had policy. Look at the result. Twelve tries scored against Warring- ton in the first seven matches ! At one time it would ;have been thought infra der for the Warrington men to resort to such a plan of defence. Apart from this it is not jiving. Let Thomas keep in the pack and help to secure possession, instead of weakening the forwards just when they need every ounce. ' After defeating Huyton last week Stockton Heath were very sanguine about their engagement with South Manchester on the home ground, and as anticipated the home side won by 4-1. The score is rather more than it should have been, when one compares the merits of the two teams on the day's play, although one must Again take into account the fact that E. E. Woods one of the Stockton full backs had to leave the field after the first ten minutes through an injured thigh.

In this match H. liirkconnel madehis first appearance for Stockton Heath this season and gave a good display both on the defence and in the art of passing and if he turns out regularly he should prove a tower of strength. The Heathens had an experiment as to how far the new off-side rule would benefit a team, playing against a side who were forced to adopt the one back game, and from the course of the play, the new rule should do a lot of good, as times without number the South for- wards would have been off side in their own half but for the new rule.

The second team met with defeat at the hands of the South Manchester second eleven on Saturday, the score being 2M in favour of the home side. But they most not lose heart, as the Mancuntans always have had a good second string, and this season have had the pick of the old Moss Side club.

He was no narrow-minded socialist in the sense that he would put all upon one common plat- form, he did not care what a man's salary was or what were his profits providing they were honestly obtained hut the first consideration was not salary or profits but the well-being of each worker and no man had right to take a salary or reap profits beyond a certain standard until every man, woman and child helping to produce the wealth of that factory or workshop was in receipt of a living wage. The solution of the unemployed problem was not impossible nay it was com- paratively easy and could be solved in less than a year if faced by sensible, earnest men. In conclusion Mr. Dunnioo appeals to all Christian people to take their share in removing these stumbling blocks so that the men who were fighting the peoples battles might feel that the true Church of God was behind them in all their highest and noblest aspirations. Loyalty to Christ involved loyalty to our fellowmen and no man could be indifferent to social questions and be consider4d a loyal servant of Jesus Christ. It was a sin to sit still while millions were being done to death by a soul destroying social system founded upon prin- ciples of selliShness.

div.head: MR. P. PEACOCWS CANDIDATURE.
div.p: MR. P. PEACOCWS CANDIDATURE.
Mr. Barnes and the Labour Party:

A well attended meeting in support of the candida- ture of Mr. P. Peacock in the Bewsey Ward was held in the Co-operative Hall,Winwick-street on Wednesday evening. Mr. Joseph Owen presided and was supported by Councillor A. Peacock, Messrs. T. Barnes, SAVright, J. Morton, and J. Howes, jun. The CHAIRMAN said that so far as was possible Mr. Peacock, since his election to the Council two years ago, had endeavoured to redeem all the promises which ibe made before he was elected. He had tried to secure the free admission of school children to the baths and Ito have cheap tickets provided for working people. The recreation ground which he advocated would be open shortly. He had striven to do all he could for the working men. (Applause.) Mr. PEACOCK, who had a hearty reception, said I several rumours had bean freely circulated in the ward with regard to his attitude towards the workingmen. : Those rumours were absolutely untrue aud in the whole of his Council experience his first consideration had been that of labour as against the higher officials. He claimed to be as much a labour man as anyone on the Council. They could not find one thing where he had not supported the labour party, and he had even gone out of his way to discuss affairs with the representatives of that party both inside and outside :the Council. He had been specially thanked by the Labour party for his services and he could not understand any opposition to his candidature from that party. (Applause.) There was an important question to come before the Council and which would have to be decided during the next month—the unemployed question. The Councilwould be called upon to carry out the unemployed act and would have to appoint a committee to do so. He particularly desired to be placed on that committee as he felt that he knew the state of employment in Bewsey Ward and the requirements of the ward. He was ie favour of absolute purity in administration and would have no "Tammany" in the Council Hale knew about it. Another great question was that of the housing of the working classes. An Act of Parliament pro- vided that aTown Council could advance to a working man the mon3y with which to nurchase his own house provided he could find one fifth of the cost price. Ile and his brother had brought forward a test case and had , failed and the Act therefore, so far as Warrington was concerned, the act was a dead letter. He was in favour of the Act being administered. If returned in November Ihe promised that he would do all be could for the pro- gress of the towns business. (Applsuse.) Mr. MORTON moved "That in the opinion of this meeting of burgesses of the Bewsey Ward Mr. Peter Peacock is a tit and proper person to represent our interests on the Town Council, and this meeting pledges itself to use all legitimate means to secure his return in the forthcoming municipal election." He understood, he said, that the project to fight Mr. Peacock with a labour candidate had fallen through. He never understood how anyone could question the fact that Liberalism always stood for laboul.. They would not stand opposition from labour, and if labour desired to make real progress they must come within the Liberal party. C.ouncillor WRIGHT seconded. He thought Councillor Peacock had from a labour standpoint, done his best on behalf of labour. It had been said that Liberal and labour could not agree. He had been a Liberal almost all his life,because he believed the cause to be the most progressive one. For 22 years he had been officially connected with labour, and during the whole of that period labour had never interfered with his Liberalism. (Applause). Mr. BARNES snpported the resolution. The action of the Labour Party in bringing out a man to oppose Mr. Peacock, he thought, spoke ill of them. (Haar, hear). He appealed to them not to listen to the party which was going about appealing to them with the voice of labour. The party was not a Labour party and their credentials were not worthy of surport. Mr, Wattut:wros : _his a tissue of falsehoods and I

can p"ro.ve it. When the last speaker said Mr. Plinston was a member of the Independent Labour Party. (A voice: He never said it"). He inferred it and is telling deliberate lies. (Cries of "order" and "sit down"). The resolution was put to the meeting and unani- mously carried. Mr. PEACOCK in returning thanks said the Independ- ent Labour Party had always been considerate towards him and some members of the psrty were a little annoyed when they heard he was being opposed by a Labour man. The Independent Labour Party had decided not to support Mr. Plinston and that rather supported what he had said about the patty being friendly to him. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: SKIN-GROWING EXTRAORDINARY.
div.p: SKIN-GROWING EXTRAORDINARY.
" Grafting" Frogs' Skins —Wonderful Achievements in Skin-Repairing.

A remarkable operation was recently performed abroad, the skin taken from forty-one frogs being "grafted "on the arms and shoulders of a woman ! The woman had sustained frightful scalds, and the skin had refused to grow over so large an area. The problem of the growth of new skin has demanded attention throughout the ages. Away back_ in the times of Ancient Greece and Home, it received more attention than it does even in this age, and so far as dealing with ordinary injuries and the prevalent skin diseases is concerned, their methods set an example to the world. _ _

The great Greeks and ROMMUS recognised that man's instinct to rub a place that hurts is Nature calling for assistance, and they answered her call by applying to the injured or diseaked part an ointment, oil, or salve, made of Nature's own rich herbal juices. These unguenta," as they were called, were so widely used that in the city of Capua a great street consisted entirely of shops in which they were sold ! The magni- ficent gladiators and athletes of that day used them regularly to heal their injuries, keep their skins healthy and maintain the general elasticity of their frames while the wealthier classes always carried costly boxes of their favourite balm with them. These were deli- cately perfumed, and their owners often anointed them- selves freely several times a day. In later centuries man has fallen into the error of using coarse preparations containing rancid anim.A fats and mineral irritants. These are too coarse to ba absorbed by tho skin, and if they could be absorbed, they would do infinitely more harm than good. It is only with the comparatively recent discovery of a new sort of calm that a return to Nature, and to the ideal methods of the great ancients has bee I successfully made. Zam-Ruk, as this new skin-cure and healer is called, is the fruit of careful research into the marvel- lous power possessed by certain rare medicinal herbs growing in tropical forests. In des course of study the exceptional curative, sooth- ing, and antiseptic properties of the extracts from these plants came to he recognised. The matter was studied closely with a view to securing the right combination of these various saps and juices, and further, to producing a preparation sufficiently concentrated and so economical as to bring it within the reach of the masses of English people. This desirable aim was at length achieved, and the introduction of Zam-buk has revolutionised the method of treating ailments and injuries of the skin. Among the unione features of Zam-buk are its herbal origin its wonderful refinement, and last, hut not least, its capacity for growing new and healthy skin. Zarn- • buk is entirely different from ordinary ointments, salves and embrocations. It is without their ohjectiorrible ingredients, and it is so wonderfully refined that the ; herbal juicer contained in it can be absorbed right through the pores of the skin, thus enabling the balm • to overcome any chronic or deep-seated affection. Ztm-huk is recommended for eczema, psoriasis, bad legs, blind and bleeding piles, running sores, ulcers, pimples, boils, rashes, chapped hands, scalp diseases, dandruff, barber's rash, raw chin alter shaving, chit- hlains, sore and aching feet, cold-sores, festering sores, ' poisoned wounds, cuts, bruises, burns, scalds, sprains, stiffness, weak ankles, swollen joints, and all diseased injured and inflamed or irritated conditions of the skin. Rubbed well in, Zam-buk kills muscular and nerve pains. Zam-Buk is sold by all chemists in one-and-three-halfpenny and two-and-nine boxes (two-and-nine size contains nearly four times the one-and-three-halfpenny), or post tree direct from the Zam-bnir Co., Red-cross-street, London, E.C. A box of this valuable balm should he kept handy in every home. I

div.head: NOVEL POSTAL CONVEYANCE.
div.p: A NOVEL POSTAL CONVEYANCE.

"To c-a-st-the.h7n7;ails upon the waters," if it be per- mitted to parody the well known proverb, appears to be the way in which the inhabitants of the Island of St. Kilda, situate on the extreme N. W. of Scotland, communicate with the outside world. The method of conveyance consists of a tin containing the letters packed in cotton wool, covered in tarred canvas, and served with twine to keep it water tight. The tin is then attached to an inflated sheep-skin bag, acting as a buoy, together with a wooden float with the words "St. Kilda Mail, please open "roughly cut on it. Quite recently a " Mail ' was picked up in Shetland which had been 62 days on its passage from St. Kilda, and, when opened, was found to contain two letters and eight postcards, together with Is. for postage. These letters were in due course fo:warded to their respective des- tinations by the post office at Lerwick. In the Case under notice, it is of much interest to note that the " Mail" was enclosed in a cocoa tin bearing the familiar name of" Van Houten's."

div.head: Warrington Win at Rochdale.
div.p: Warrington Win at Rochdale.

The first round of the Lancashire Cup drew Warring- ton to plsy the Hornets at Rochdale, which town they visited with a good deal of confidence. Fish and Ken- yon were both absentees, while the Hornets were short of Blencon, their best threequarter. Wet weather pre- vailed, a fine rain falling continuously, so that the con- e'itions were all against good football not more than 1,00 spectators assembled. Teams . _

Rochdale Tiornets—W. Rig (cant.) back; A. .1. Richardson, F. Fielding, A. G. Charles, and A. Gibson, three-quarter backs ; R. Schofield and T. Kiley, half backs ; A. Turner, F. Lord, W. Wood, F. Crabtree, W. Richardson, A. Thomas, A. Brooks, and J. Bearden, forwards.

Warrington—Knight, back ; Jordan, Dickenson, Isherwood, and Harris, three-quarter backs ; Brooks and Hockenhall, half backs ; Boardman, Preston, Thomas, Harmer, Swift, Jolley, Beitou. and Cook, forwards. Referee, Mr. F. Kennedy, Broughton Rangers ; and Messrs. A. Lee (Leigh) and H. Broome (Oldham)touch judges. Rigg commenced operations against the wind, and the visitors rushed to the home half, where Jordan re- ceived and raced to the line, but Rigg brought him down. Smart work by Rigg transferred play to the centre, and several dashes by the Hornets saw the War- rington line in danger. The Warrington men now attacked vigorously, and Rigg repeatedly put in some tine defensive work. The Warrington pack eventually rushed the ball over the line, and Schofield saved by touching down. Harris ran down touch and kicked across, Harmer scoring near the posts and Preston land- a goal. Half time—Warrington 1 goal 1 try (5 points), Hornets nil. On the re-start Fielding and Charles:took play to the visitors' 25, where Warrington were penalised, but Rigg failed. Gibson received from a fumble by Jordan, but the latter brought him down in the nick of time. Schofield next made a dash for the line, and Warrington were having their work cut out to keep their line intact. A miss by Charles let Warrington invade for the first time this half, after 20 minutes' play, but Richardson repulsed them. Itigg and Gibson played well for the home team, but eventually the Warrington backs prlssed splendidly and Isherwood scored behind the post, Preston improving. Result :—Warrington 2 goals 2 tries (10 points), Rochdale Hornets, nil.

div.head: League Match on Monday.
div.p: League Match on Monday.
Bradford Well Beaten.

Warrington returned to League football on Monday when they met Bradford before a gate of nearly 3,000. The visitors were without Marsden, while Warrington played practically the same team as at Rochdale. Excellent weather prevailed and the Wilderspool ground WAS in perfect order. Teams : Warrington—Knight, back; 3 ordnn, Isherwood, Dickenson. and Harris, three-quarter hacks ; Hocken- ball and Brooks, half backs ; Preston, Thomas, Cook, Belton, Jolley, Harmer, Boardman, and Forster, for- wards.

Bradford—Floyec, back ; Dechan, Gunn, Mosby, and Connell, three-quarter backs ; Wilson and Brear- half backs ; Laidlaw, Salales, Sharratt, Francis, Rees, Feather, Turner, and Greenwood, forwards. Referee, Mr. Oakland,Outwood : touch judges,Messrs. Edwards, St. Helens, and Underwood, Wigan. Warrington played against the wind in the fist half Boyes early on almost let in the home forwards. but a speedy recovery was forthcoming, and some capital exchanges between Knight and Boyes took place. The game was carried on at a fast rate, and several brilliant expositions of passing were given by both sides. By the aid of tall kicking Warrington got dangerous, only to find the Bradford defence sound. Excellent passing was shown by Brooks and Isherwood, and for sometime Bradford were penned in their " 25." Harris made a big effort after splendid passing, Boyes effecting a fine tackle at the corner flag. Warrington maintained the pressure, and Dickenson, taking a cross kick from Jordan, scored behind the posts, Preston adding the goal. Dickenson was hurt, and compelled to retire. Warrington still attacked strongly, Knight frustrating all efforts of Bradford to invade. Near the interval the visitors pressed, but Knight maintained his good form, and at half-time Warrington led by 5 points to nil. Bradford started with great vigour and the forwards nearly rushed the hall over in the first minute, Hocken- ball cleared to centre, where some floe play was seen. The home halves opened the game out very smartly and Bradford were hard pat to to check the incursions of the home backs. In the struggle, Wilson got hurt and retired, leaving the teams equal again in numbers. Soon after, Hockenhall raced away splendidly and though tackled on the line he threw back to Preston who scored a try and kicked a goal. Decban improved matters for the visitors and a spell of severe scrummaging ensued on the home line. Knight finany kicked clear, and a beautiful effort by Brooks eind Thomas deserved a better fate. Warrington kept up the attack and Harris raced over at the corner, no goal resulting. In the closing stages Bradford made a great effort to score and Denham was tackled by Thomas only a font short of the line. Final: Warrington 2 goals 3 tries (13 points), Bradford, nil.

THE GREAT BEAR,
FLORENCE WARDEN (Author rf" The .ITouse on the 3far.Nh." " A Patched up .etyilir," 4c.)

lite platform at huston Station was alive with passengers, hurrying, scurrying hither and thither amidst the usual turmoil of departure : porters were yelling By'r leave !' and then without leave running into nervous old ladies, while dogs yapped, and babies screamed, and excited passengers rushed wildly between lthe train, the bookstall and the refreshment-room. _

The Northern Express was frantically puffing out its eagerness to start, for the last five minutes had come, when 'two girls, the elder very pretty and fragile-looking, and the younger neither the one nor the other, came quickly towards the train, with an attendant sporter, looking for a seat. It was the month of July, and seats in every train that went out of London were at a pre- mium.

"Here you are, Miss," said the porter, as be opened the door of a compartment in which there were indeed two vacant places, but from out of which there scowled the face of a stolid-looking, thick-set Englishman, clean-shaved save for a small side-*hisker, whose tweed suit and cap to match were brand•new, and something in whose look and manner, as well as in the appearance of his bags and papers, proclaimed the lawyer. The moment the porter placed on the opposite seat to him the cushion which he was carrying, and backed out to make way for the young ladies, the passenger in the tweed suit, with a black scowl, seized his bags and his papers, his rug and his gun-case, and bounced out of the carriage. And the younger of the two girls, not the tall and pretty one, saw him seize a passing porter, and rapidly command him to find him another place, adding : " They've rammed an invalid into the carriage where I was : and I hate invalids, especially women invalids." " Bear !" cried the girl, under her breath, but yet not so low but that the passenger caught the word as be turned his head suddenly, and ex- changed a brief look with her.

It"was a look of fierce disdain on the girl's side, of stubborn, devil-may-care non-apology on his. And then Jenny Mulgrave, with her head very high in the air, sat down opposite to her delicate sister, and busied herself in making her as comfortable as possible for their long journey. For Mary. the elder, had been vary ill while staying in London with their father, a Colonel on foreign service who had come home to spend part of his leave with them. Colonel Mulgrave had now returned to his regiment, and the two girls, who had been motherless for many years, were on their way back to their home with their 'aunt, who had x cottage near Ambleside. A sad enough journey this was, for besides their natural sorrow at having to say good-bye to their father, pretty Mary had a heart-trouble to bear, and the place she was going back to was haunted with the saddest memories for her.

Besides being sad, the journeY. P-r-ot;il;ed to be unpleasant. The day was not only intensely hot, but windy besides. And an old lady who sat at the other end of tits compartment, with her back to the engine, insisted on having the window down as far as it would go, with the result that thick clouds of dust and blacks from the engine came in upon all the passengers. And then, to crown all, the disagreeable man in the tweed suit came in again at Rugby, and having lost his former seat, now placed himself in the corner facing the old lady and at once pulled up the window. Excuse ;me," said she, immediately letting it down again, " but I muss have air." " I am sorry to cause you inconvenience, madam," replied the disagreeable man firmly. " but I cannot be suffocated with dust, and as am on the weather side, I believe I have the right to decide whether the window is to be up or down."

" Whatever your rights may be, sir," retorted the old lady indignantly, "as a gentleman, if you are a gentleman, it is your duty to give way to a lady." " I know nothing about ladies or gentlemen, madam," retorted he, firmly. "I allow that a man ought to give way to a woman on any poin where his sex gives him an undue advan- tage. But in the matter of the swallowing of a cartioad of (lust and grit, the throat and lungs of a man are no less susceptible than those of a woman. I am sorry that I must insist on not being choked."

There was a distinct feeling of satisfaction throughout the carriage at this speech, and Jenny Mu'grave felt quite angry at being com- pelled, against her will, to take the part of • the bear against the old lady. Everybody began unconsciously to look to the strong-minded stranger for further entertainment ; but from that point he wrapt himself up in his news- papers, and in the perusal of bundles of blue pipers, and in no way made himself further conspicuous. _ _

In the meantime the sky had clouded over, the thunder had begun to multer' and the light- ning to glimmer faintly ; and by the time the: girls had to get out of the train at the junction for Windermere, a fierce storm was raging and the wind had begun to blow a hurricane.

There were only a few passengers going on to Windermere and among the number was the of whom the sisters spoke under their bie th as the great bear.' By the time the terminus was reached, and the girls got out, poor Mary was so utterly worn out that it was with difficulty that Jenny helped lier nut, and staggered with her across the plat- form.

As Mary was very tall, and Jenny was rather short, they got on pretty badly ; and Jenny bad, against her will, to feel almost grateful when ' the bear ' with a curt • Allow me,' took the fainting Mary by the arm on the other aide, and rather carried than led her across the platform to the outer door of the station.

"How are you going on ?" asked he, in a tone H 8 abrupt as ever, of Jenny, as he still sup- ported her faintly remonstrating sister. " Well, we were going by the coach, but now I think we'd better take a cab," began Jenny, with a troubled face. . . .

For Mary looked so ill that she wondered whether she could bear the five miles' drive through the storm. Look here," said ' the beer,' after a mo- Input's pause, during which Mary's face grew perceptibly whiter and whiter, " if you'll take my advice you'll take her into one of the hotels here, and give her some brandy and water, and have your tea, and wait till this storm is over. Then you can drive along comfortably in the evening, without so much risk of being swept away.'' " Yes, yes, thank-you, thank-you. That will be best," said Jenny. "I— W9—'' But before she could make up her mind what she was going to say or do, the stranger had hailed a cab, lifted Mary into it, and after turn- ing to Jenny and learning the name of the hotel she wished to drive to, put her in also, and raising his hat as he shut the door, said : " I shall come on there myself and see that you're all tight." " Thank-you, oh thank—" _ . .
But he was gene, and Jenny. bewildered. turned to her sh.ter, and maid, in an atvectruck voice :
" The bear la barna! after all, isn't be *:"

Mary nodded, without paying much attention. Travelling rather too soon after a tedious i 1 nes, she was 80 much exhausted that she was scarcely more than half c4nsciom4 of what silo wee doiug when she was led into OM tile].

"We haven't a pri rate room vacant," said the manager, to whom old M ims Mid grave and her nieces were well-linown. " Will you go into the coffee-room ? There's no one there." So Jenny lea ber 14,4 er into the long, Lright moth, niada Mary lie isiek iii R big easy chair. br who. ~ho for. a cup of tea.
Man can live 100 years

The convalescent IVIO4 lying bum at enact Irma her eyes closed, end Jseny bad gone softly to the window to peep out behind the draw,i bqua., at ti' flashing Egi,t,d,:g mid OA swasitn.r trees, when she beard hOnitlAle COMO into tito room, and looking round, saw that t• the Fear " uvai standing still on the hearthrug, gazing intently at Mary. His eyes met Jenny's, and be smiled a little ; she thought his wooden face looked rather nice when he smiled, !icing perbaps incltio-al to feel complimentary rifler his kindness at be station. Then he nodded and came across the room to her with ostentatiously quiet footsteps. " She's gone to sleep," said he. " That'll do her good. Don't disturb her ; have your tea comfortably, while she's resting, and presently she'll wake up RR fresh as a daisy. Let me ring the hell and order you some tea." He crossed the room again, and rang the bell, returning to her immediately. " It's very kin—" began Jenny. But he cut her short with a wave of the hand. . . _

" Not a bit, not a bit. I owe you some re- paratiOn, y,,u know," he went on, sti.ll brusque- ly, but with a half-smile of shy apology, end good-humoured British ItWkwordneBs. " I'm afraid you heard a stupid and ill-tempered re- mark of mine at Easton ; I didn't mean what I said a hit, of course, and I deserve to be kicked for having uttered it at all ; but if you'll " take it out " in any little services I can render you and your pretty sister, I shall be only too de- lighted, believe me."

, The was rough manner was so frank, such evident kindliness of nature peeped out under all his shy ruggedness, that Jenny looked full at him with a bright smile which showed that he was forgiven. He made her wrap a light rug round her sleep- ing sister, had a swan tire lighted for fear she should suffer from the chill in the atmosphere which had followed the out break of the storm and the persistent downpour. and finally when the waiter brought in his and Jenny's tea on the same tray, he naked her, with another shy smile, whether she would permit him to sit at the same table with her.

" The waiter does Ine the honour to think' be- long to your party," said he, " but I'm such an old buffer I don't think you need mind. I know already that you're the Misses Ma!grave, that your aunt is a lady very much respected in the neighbourhood : the landlady told me so. And now I ought to tell you that my name's L;ridley, Richard 'Gridley, and that I don't know that I'm much respected anywhere, because I'm only lawyer, and everybody knows that lawyers are the chosen children of the Old Gentleman down- stairs don't they ?" "I don't know about that," said Jenny, laughing, as she took lier eeat at the table. " I don't think I've ever known much about them."
..... " Well, take my advice, and don't try to know any more," said Richard Gridley promptly, as be seated himself in him turn at the table.

" I suppose they're not all wicked," said Jenny, smiling. "My father puts the greatest confidence in his lawyer, I know." " Great mistake !" said Gridley, as, bearing the girl in the chair behind him move slightly, he turned to look at her.

But Mary was still -sleeping, making a touch- ingly beautiful picture, with her disordered fair hair shown up against the red morocco leather of the chair, and the dark eyebrows and eyelashes that looked almost black against her dead-white skin.

" Your sister's very handsome !" whispered Mr. Gridley solemnly. " You won't be able to keep her long. There will come some dashing young fellow after her, and you'll want a cur- mudgeon like me to draw up the marriage settle. !tient."
" Oh, no," cried Jenny, impulsively, " her hesrri broken !"

Aud then she bit her lip, dreadfully ashamed of her unnecessary frankness to a stranger. She was surprised at herself too, but there was Nomad) ing which seemed to her to invite traq in to rugged man when once his feelings were touched, as they bad been by Mary's indisposi- tion.

But the very next moment be Pa id something which made her rise up in arms against him. " You said it was typhoid she had had," he objected bluntly. " Typhoid comes from bad drainage, not from a broken heart." .• . .

" If-Efie hadn't been made susceptible by 1111. Imppiness, she wouldu't have caught it," said she tartly. Mr. Gridley shrugged his shoulders. " Oh, well," he said, " I suppose you know best. But there, there, never mind. She'll get over it : she's much too pretty to be allowed to grieve long." Jenny shook her head. . _ _ _
" She isn't fickle, like other girls," said she proudly. " She would never marry to got mar- ried, ftll other girls do : it will be the num of her heart, or it will be hone." _
Mr. Gridley looked at.bia torte.
" Ah, well." he said, " I don't know much about such things, except in the way of business. I'm here on an affair of that sort now.'
" Indeed ?"

" Yes." There WM a pause, during which Jenny poured herself out another cup of tea. `4 Marriages are ruin things," he then added. " Lawyers must see the worst side of a good many things," said Jenny after another pause, not being ready with any snore appropriate re- mark, mid observing that his tone denoted that he took an unfavourable view of the matter. " Yes, I suppose they do. Especially of mar- riage. Yet the experience of others doesn't keep them away from it themselves." And lie added dreamily : " Now speaking of myself, for in- stance, I wonder whether I shall be able, in the long run, to hold out against the besetting temp- tation to which HO Matlya lawyer succumbs --" " What temptation's that P" asked Jenny, see- ing that he waited, and with a twinkle in his eye which suggested that he was ready to be ques- tioned.

Why, the temptation of marrying his cook !" " What ?" cried Jenny, bursting into a laugh. Ho nodded gravely. " Oh, yes, it seems to me to be quite an irre- sistible one ! I've known scores of respectable solicitors succumb to it. They haven't time to go about and look for a wife, I suppose, so they take the first woman to hand : and of course that's the cook. I've often looked at Mrs. Biggs— that's the name of mine—she's a most worthy ii.rson, but rotund of figure, and at least fifty, and not what you'd call good-looking at that." While Jenny tried in vain to restrain her laugh- ler, lie went on more gravely than ever : " And I look at her, and I look, when I send for her to about the bacon, and I think to myself, Shall I ever come to that ?' And I say, No- on, I won't.' But then I remember the scores of other solicitors who must have said the same thing to themselves about their cooks, and I con- fess I tremble l" Now Jenny laughed so uncontrollably at this and at the droll gravity with which Mr. Gridley said it, that she woke her sister, who started up in a dazed way, and asked what was the matter. Thin storm having by this time abated a little, and Mary feeling much better and ready for the drive, a cab was ordered at once, and the girls collected their wraps and bags and prepared to start.

"By the bye," paid Mr. Gridley, Re he in. eimted on taking their small articles of luggage for theta to the cab, " you are residente in tide part of the world. rerhapß you can tell me in which direction lieversham Hall lies ?"

Both girls started. and Mary's white face flushed. Jenny uttered a low cry. "Is it about Percival's marriage you have come F" she asked quickly. And while be hesitated, and stammered, and saw what an unfortunate speech be had made, Mary walked on towards the cab without a word " 'Dear, dear," said Mr. Gridley, " r don't know what to say ! I'm afraid I've unintention- ally put tny foot in it again. I suppose I needn't ask—That was the—"

" Oh, may don't arty any more about it," • raid Jenny sharply, as she followed her sister. And, though she tried to thank him again for Iris kind. attentions, when he shut the cah-door for them, neither she nor poor Mary could help holding their heads very high, and speaking with a perceptible chilliness, when they knew they were addressing the very man who had come 10 arrange the business of the wedding of faithless Percival Heversham with another won an. Mary bore the drive home Fret:, well, mil Miss Mulgraye, their aunt, a placid ohi. lady, who did not let small things :',lsturb her, merely remarked that they were rather late, and then despatched the in valid to bud. ..,enny eat up thinking. It was quite true that ...ao believed her sister's heart to be broken by the rupture with Percival Heversham, land she dreaded this return to the scenes that must recall to Mary the happy days she bad spout there, when she thought she was to be the wife of the man who had gained her heart. Angry as Jenny could not help feeling will' Percival, she knew that he lied heen placed in a 7.2ry difficult nosition. by no fault of his cam in

rewstra to- are marriage. Laay neverstiain, his mother, was a greedy, ambitious woman, the chief Object of whose life was to make up for the reduction her srendthrift husband had made in the family fortune by marrying all her childreo " well." Now the marriage of her second lino handsomest son, Percival, to a girl of no foam,. ; but her beautiful face, she regarded as a mimfor- tune to be avoided at all coats. And she bad treated Mary with so much coldness, if not abso- lute rudeness, since Percival declared his engage ment, that the proud girl had had no alterneivi but to break off the match herself, even though she broke her own heart at the same time. ; So on leaving Windermere for London two inontlis before this, she had written to Percival, ' telling him- that she could not enter a family where she would be unwelcome, and begging him to consider their engagement at an end. He bad indeed written bask, begging her to- reconsider ' her decision, as he was ready to wait and work for her, even if his mother treated them badly and would afford them no help. Mary had been ; inexorable ; and so the matter had ended. _ _ _ _

Bat though Mary and her sister both under- stood this to be an irrevocable decision, it now came an a shock upon both to find that, so 9010• after. Percival was on the 'eve of marriage • another lady. Miss Mulgrave, their aunt, had heard all about it, but had thought it better not to write the news.

"It's all Lady Heversham's doing, of course," she said to Jenny that evening. • The woman he's to marry is an American widow, nearly old enough to be his mother, as yellow as leather, and with a voice that grates on one to hear. But she's very rich, they say, and so there's nothing more necessary. But they do say," and she looked sombrely at the lampshade, and shook her head, " that the poor boy's not himself at all." "I don't think much of a man who lets him- self be married against his will 1" said Jenny scornfully. " It's the sort of thing a real man, a strong man, would never do."

And Instinctively she thought of Mr. Gridley. The next morning, before she was up, Jenny heard the gallop of a horse, and a dead stop cot- side the garden gate. Before she was wide enough awake to wonder who the early visitor was, she heard the horse galloping away again. And then, as it was still very early, she went off to sleep once more. Invalid as Mary was, she was down first that morning • restless, miserable, excited, she could not lie still, and before anyone else was about, she was out in the little bit of garden in the front of the house.

When Jenny went downstairs in her turn, she met her sister, not the pale spectre she had been uNed to of late, but a radiant, smiling creature, hugging to her breast a great bunch of bright garden and hothouse flowers.
Why, where did you get those P" asked Jenny, amazed. _ _

'‘ They were outside—in the porch !" whis- pered Mary. breathlessly. "Oh, Jenny, it must have been Percival who brought them! Look at the long sprays of plumbago : it doesn't grow like that anywhere but at Heversham Hall !" Jenny WAS struck dumb. She remembered the galloping horseman, and wondered whether it eould really have been Percival Heversham who had come thus early in the morning to pay a surreptitious homage to the girl he had been compelled to give up. She would not express any doubts : she had not the heart to do so, and tp disturb her sister's sweet dream. But when, on the following morn- she woke early, and set herself to watch at her window, as the first mound of a galloping- horse reached her ear, she was more shocked than surprised to find that it was Mr. Gridley, who jumped off at the gate, walked quickly up the garden, and disappearing into the porch With handful of freshly out flowers in his hand, pre. mealy reappeared and rode off without them. He did it all in a shamefaced way, with an odd sort of shy, devil-may-care, you-may-iiee-me-inakieg a-fool-of-myself-if-you-like manner, which made Jenny laugh to herself. But she was troubled too : for though alio liked " the bear," and indeed admired him much more than a man of the Percival Hevornham type her.elf, she had considerable doubts whether Mary would ever transfer her liking from the faithless Pereival.to the rugged solicitor. Jenny made au attempt to find out whether Mary in any way reciprocated the admiral inn w !deli Mr. Gridley had expressed for her. But alie was scornful and made light of the notion. " That horrid, rough creature, whom you yourself named the bear I' How can you risk if I could ever like him P" said she, with her head held very high. Jenny drew herself up.
" I think he's much more of a man than Per- cival Hover/them," retorted she, " who hasn't the manliness to make a fight for the • girl lie loves."

"You don't know the difficulties he may be in," mid Mary softly. And she added in a hur- ried whisper : "Do you know I have a fancy if rill all come right? That he's preparing the way with these flowers ?”

" But supposing it isn't lie who brings the dowers at all ?" suggested Jenny. " Why don't you watch, and find out r she added quickly. But Mary, who had the excuse that her room was at the back of the house, with no window on the front, would not do this. Perhaps she was afraid, Jenny limited, with a pang for the gen- tle, senmitive heart. They met both Percival Heversharn and Mr. Gridley about the neighbourhood several times in the course of the next few days. Both the men raised their hats and passed on, leaving the girls in considerable agitation. And still Jenny could not raise her courage to the point of opening Mary's eyes as to her self-deception. At last one day it happened that Jenny was walking back alone from the post-office, when she catne face to face with Mr. Gridley as she turned a corner. She was thinking about him, and the meeting startled her so much that she eri,l " Oh !" bob iv her breath.

Mr. Gridley reddened, raised his hat, passed her. and then ran after her. " May I speak to you ?" said he. Then, with- out waiting for permission, he accommodated his pace to hers. " What would you give me," he asked ab- ruptly, "if I were to make it all right between your sister and young Heveraham P" Jenny started and stared at him. " Why," cried she, " I thought that you—l —I—I—I mean—wasn't it you who brought the flowers for her P" It was Mr. Gridley's turn to redden. " For her !" he said rather blankly. "Why, why, did you think—" And then he began to talk about the weather : and be talked of nothing else till he raised his hat and went away. Now this singular interview set Jenny think log, but Rho said nothing about it to her sister or her aunt. When, however, about a week later, she saw Mr. Gridley and Percival Fleversham walking sedately up the garden-path together, she started to her feet, and timing to the other two ladies, who were sit ling in the drawing room wiiii.har, said, hurriedly, in a low voice : . -

- - " They're come ! It's going to be all right." Now neither Diary nor her a nut hail ',eon the vi.ilorm approaching., and neither had the least idea what die meant. Therefore, when, a mo- ment later, the two gentlemen were ahown into the room, it was Jenny alone who appeared quite componed. Mr. Gridley had to IA Introduced to Miss Mul- grit and trivialitien had to be talked al out for Home minute:4. But presently Percival founa an opportunity of following Mary to the other end of the room, where (hey had interesting explana- tion to exchange, while Mr. Gridley drew nearer to the other two ladies, and did his own _

...you have to Mink me for brinzing hi here," he said in a low voice, " if you're Rind to see him beck. AS the son of SS OM friend of hi., tither's, I very soon SSW, On my orrice!, diet ti 08 marriege the old holy Irol errnozed botiviieti him and the widow you have heard of, wollnl Its" term Meg fortittimfr sin she Wei domineering, she would have made the lad miserable. So 1 put it to him, and presently I put it to Lady Ileversham, and last of all, I put it to the lady herself that the whole thing Wes a mistake. And having in the meantime been able to assure the lad that his suit some- where else would have a very good ehace if it wore renewed, I carried thin through so nicely I hat—that, well, its you see, I've made it all right with Lady Heversham, we've got rid of the widow, and—and here he is !" "I guessed how it would end." smiled old Miss Mulgrave. " Why, Mr. Gridley, the dear buy's been leaving flowers for her every morn- ing !" At that point Mr. Gridey's eye caught Jenny's, and both looked promptly down on the carpet. Both were curiously red. But when they had ell had tea, pleasantly chatting in the lung, low drawing room, with the windows wide open, and the bees humming outside, Mr. Gridley managed to have an ex- Ilia neon
