div.head: MT DEAR CRILDREN;
div.p: MT DEAR CRILDREN;

I have received a great many letters from some of you during this week, and have pub- lished a few of the best below. I have also had several little stories sent me to be put into the "Children's Corner"; these are very pretty little tales, and nicely composed. A little later on I shall offer a special prize for the best atoryette sent me, and, of course, it shall be published in these columns. I am glad to hear from my nephew, A. Knight, that .he was pleased with the prize sent him. At present I have not received any list of names. You will remember I offered a post-card album to any of you sending me ,two dozen names of new members; but I dare say it takes a long time to get these lists filled in, as most of you are at school all the day: I will say good-bye for this week. With all good wishes, from • Yours affectionately, UNCLE NED.'

Dear Uncle Ned,—l received my watch by post in a neat little box from R. L. Chrietie, Edinburgh, as per instruction from you yester- day, September 31, 1.905, and I am very pleased with it, and shall prize it very much as a memento of the "Children's Corrier League," and when I look at it I am reminded of the motto also for 1905:'" I pass through this world but once, therefore any good deed that I can do let, me do it now, for I shall not pass this way again." I hope not only to learn the motto, but to act upon it, and wish all friends to do the same, and also try to win the prizes from time to time. When I competed I did not ex- pect to win, but I was determined to do my best and try; and, my little brother 'and sister, also, you must expect, will get two dozen names for the "Children's Corner," and win one of the post-card albums offered by you. I wish all my little friends •success, and especially the "Children's Corner League." I read the stories each week, and like to do so; they are so in- teresting. Should you think, Uncle Ned, that the watch should be placed in the Office window for the nephews and nieces of Uncle Ned to see? I shall be,glad to do so for one week, that all may be encouraged to work for the "Children's Corner League," and help to get the thousand members required. Thank- ing you very much for the prize received by • Your affectionate nephew, ERNEST R. DoNEY.

My Dear Uncle Ned,—l wish to become a member of .the "Children's Corner League," and I will try my very best to get others to join. I have tried my very best to do the puzzles which are in this week's paper. I have enclosed an envelope for you to please send me some forms. I would like very much to have a post-card .album of nay own. I have only done the first tw6 puzzles, as I don't quite understand the Word square. I will close now, with best wishes. Your loving niece,
MAY AVERY.

Uncle .tied,—As I wish to become a member of your League, I will tell you about my to pet bantams. These birds are prize ones. The cock has taken first and special prizes. My special prize was a two-blade pocket-knife given by "Pearson's Weekly." The hen was "highly commended." They are "Old English Game" birds. I can feed them from my hands. I think your little stories and recitations very nice. I am company sergeant in the Boys' Brigade in this town. With my best wishes for You and the League, •
I remain', Yours truly, HERBERT KING.

div.head: CAPTAIN DUCK. (Continued.)
div.p: CAPTAIN DUCK. (Continued.)

Every Vme that Big Dan, the stage driver. cattle by, he would make all sOrts of fun ol Captain .Duck, as he hobbled about and hitched up the four stage horses, While the driver sat high up in the box and snapped his long whip. The Indian did not like Big Dan, and Big Dan did not like the Indian. Dan said the Indian was a spy, and told the men at the stage station that some night Captain Duck would set fire to the place and run away by the light of the blaze. One hot day, as he sat on the box with the four lines in his hand all ready to start off at a gallop down the great mountain, he told the Indian, with an oath, to "waddle in on his duck legs" and get liinz a drink. The Indian did not move. Then Da:n struck him with his whip. The men standing around roared with laughter. Still the sad-faced cripple did not move. Then Dan struck him another cut, across the face. The Indian's brow grew dark and; terrible, but he did not stir. Some one else brought the drink, and then, the driver snapping his whip, the stage dashed away down the moun- tain and left the Indian standing there, with the boy tenderly wiping his friend's bleeding face and speaking kind and pitiful words to him. The two friends went up on the moun- tain-side by the little pine grove, and watched the horses as before, and the Indian never spoke at all of what had happened. *, A month or two went by, and everybody for- got about the trouble between Big Dan and the sad-faced savage. Everybody, did I say? One day the stage came thundering in with Big Dan the driver leaning forward helpless on the box. There had been a shot fired from the thick wood back upon the mountain-side. The man was dying, and. the four reins were slipping through his helpless hands. Who could have fired that shot? When the stage driver was dead and buried, some of the men took Limber Tim aside and asked him whether he had been all the time with Captain Duck the day the shot was fired. "All the time, every minute, every seoond," answered the lad, earnestly. For he had no suspicion. at all that Captain Duck had shot the stage driver. Indeed, the boy believed what he said, and would have maintained it at any hazard. He forgot that he had fallen asleep on the warm, fiat rock that cool autumn day.

The next summer, signal-fires were seen one night on the mountain-tops. The men at the stage station hastened to fasten the old log fort. For this, they knew, meant war. The Modocs were on the war-path. (To be continued.)

div.head: CHRISTIAN CITIZENSHIP.
div.p: CHRISTIAN CITIZENSHIP.
Some Much-Needed Reforms. • Sermon By the Rev. John Yonge.

Preachingat Wycliffe Church on Sunday evening, the _lev. John 'Yong° took for his subject "Every day duties of Christian citizenship." His address was based on the text" The glory of God did lighten it," which !he said presented a vision of the Celestial future ! which we delighted to gaze upon. Instead of ! dreaming of the Heaven which was in the future, he thought the passage suggested that Christian I believers should combine to make the earth somewhat ! Heavenly; that each should do his little towards making- the city of his abode a purer,' and happier place in which to dwell. On all hands there was a steadily extending arousal to the necessity and the duty of Christian people interesting themselves in the general welfare of the community. Sometimes there seemed to be an idea that the duty of citizenship was fulfilled by voting at election, but that was not the only . duty. The Christian citizen needed to be an ! active and continual force for righteousness ' seeking ways and opportunities in which he I might serve the general good, promoting th,e welfare of the whole community, Tennyson, in ; some!of his happiest lines, forecasted the time of uni- versal human prosperity, and in his words, " Then shall ! all men's good be each man's rule," they, had the ger- ! minal principle of unselfish living:\ 'There they had the true goodness in active and continual display ; each man and woman governed and inspired by the desire to make life good for those who are around them ; every- one filled with the desire to make the place in which he dwelt the better for his life, and the people among whom he daily mingled the happier and healthier for his presence. If a town was to be kept clean, healthy, and happy, it depended surely upon each inhabitant doing his share towards making it so, yet how many people were there who seemed to think that they bad no call to trouble themselves about their neigh- ; beers ? Surely it was an everyday duty of the Christian citizen to do all he could in further- ance of the cause of right and truth among his fellows. These were fine words of the ancient I prophet, Zechariah, who said to his people in the name of Jehovah: "These are the things that ye shall do : Speak every man the truth to his neighbour! Execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates ! Let none of you imagine evil in your hearts against his neighbour, and love no false oath • for all these things I hate, saith the Lord !" If the Christian citizen lived on those lines be would always be on the side of God and of goodness, and he would set himself resolutely against anything and everything that cbuld lower the tone or deteriorate the life of a town. It appeared to him that there were many ways in which this could be done in Warrington. For example, could not our people do something to check the Sunday trading that was so increasintly prevalent? He had even heard of I cases in which Christian people, members of I churches and chapels, had their shops, not open, hut accessible on Sunday, and that they defended the I practice on the ground that if they kept the shop door locked on Sundays they would stand to lose custom on the other days. 'Good Christian citizenship, he thought could effect desirable reform in that matter. Again, could their. Christian people do nothing to check the evil language which So characterized the frequent talk of the thoroughfares. A few months ago, at a P.S.A. meeting in the Co-operative Hall, he took the oppor- tunity of uttering a protest against the profane swear- ing that was so rife. He tried to illustrate its slily absurdity often ;as well as its not infrequent filthy vileness. The youth of both sexes madeuse of expres- sions which ought to be banished from all talk that claimed to be civilized. In that there was a wide field of usefulness' in which some' of them might find plenty of 'valuable work as Christian eitizeas. There was great need for a crusade in this direction. 'Warrington streets, especially on Saturday and Sunday nights, would be pleasanter to pass along if the talk, the slang and the profanity could be purged away. Zechariah, speaking of the time when Jerusalem should be called" a city of truth," said : " And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in the I streets thereof." Bishop Phillips Broos, of America, I said of that text " What a wonderful civic life will ! there be in Gott's city ! The streets fit for children, and the children fit for the streets." But our streets, unhappily, were yet a long way off any such condition. . lie was often distressed by the gangs of youths and girls who walked in noise and disorder in the town, I especially on the dark winter Saturday mid Sunday j nights. ehristian parents should seek to exercise a little more control over the freedom of their young people than was sometirnee the case. Our streets, unhappily, core not the beat promenades for our youths, end especially for our girls, and Christian men of municipal &lice and influence should, it seemecie to him, seek to care something more than they did for the orderly behaviour of the public thoroughfares. Perhaps he might also be permitted to utter a word of protest en another point. The hoerdings were sometimes largely I covered by theatrical picture placards, which always I gathered groups of young people. His criticism was directed against one very prominent lied undesirable feature of some of those placards. It would seem that it was,an attraction to the theatre to placard a tragic event—robbery, suicide or . murder—in which revolvers anti daggers figured. Was not this infinitely undesirable? It must engender evil thought, and influence evil imagination; and familiarize the ignorant and unthinking mind with the wrong. He had often thought it should be in the province of the I Corporation or the education authority to create a ! censorship of these placards. They seemed to him to be detrimental to the moral health of the town, and especially of its youth. How could it elevate anybody to see, pictorially presented, diabolic murder, or some ghastly tragedy,' even though it might be warningly presented as the Outcome of some vicious course? Good Christian citizenship, be thought, would do something . towards the removal of such demoralizing exhibitions ! Passing now to another phaso of his large subject, it should be the Min of Christian citizens to secure the best and most Christian men as members of the ruling atitholities, but it by 'no means found general fulfil- ' ment, very largely because so many of the most com- petent citizens declined the duty, for various reasons.. They could not gite the time. They did not desire the responsibility. They did not like the treat- , ment sometimes encountered. The control of the community ought to! be in the hands of its Lest men, men nut necessarily of the best social posi- tion, but of tho best probity, of the best honour, the best truthfulnesseand the best and most unquestionable ! unseltlshaess. A Christian man could do as Christian a work in the Town Council or on the magisterial bench , as in the church or the Sunday school. Such men were needed in the Council chamber and in the town offices. They were needed there as everywhere else " to let ! their light shine " 'away the darkness which otherwise ! might prevail. Public 'life needed uplifting, purifying, ! Christianizing. The MuniCipal Act which obtained In , London differed from that iti the provinces, and hence in more than one of the boroughs into which the , Metropolis was now divided the Mayor was a Christian I minister. Tho Mayor of 15lary1ebone, for instance, was the Rev. Russell Wakefield, a vicar of one of the local churches. He wage man of broad and liberal views, and had shown his breadth by taking his alderman and councillors tea Nonconformist church. A few months ago he add eased a large congre- gation of working men in Hengler's Circus in London one Sunday afternooo. His theme was "Civic responsi- bility." He dealt with it from the Christian standpoint, and said he" regarded ail government as a trust front God. Sacrifice for brother man was the true key note of civic life. Si, long as one man or woman was hurt in manhood or in womanhood, so long as one child goes hungry to a State school, so long as one poor wayfarer drops to death through starvation or exposure, so long as one honest ban or woman cries for work and cannot get it, so long as one home is fetid and inaanitary, so ion.' as one life is stunted for which the State should find bread, so long nmst one work in this world keeping as it were an everlasting and divine discontent until the kingdom of the world ,s the kingdom of Christ." That was the Christian view of Christian citizenship. Let that b. I accepted, worked upon, applied to all the mairlitions of civil life, and t'ee dawn of the better day would be at band, when even on this earth it would be true of the city " lhe gldry of God did lighten it."

div.head: GOLD MINING IN EGYPT.
div.p: GOLD MINING IN EGYPT.

:Ic...cording to Mr. C. J. Alford, the Consulting Engineer of the Egyptian Mines Exploration Company, who, as Vice-President of the Institution of Mining and Metallurgy, should know what he is talking about wartre on the ova oran Egyptian gold mining boom. Certainly the developments in the land of the Pharaohs are remarkable. Nile Valley has turned out some k:(10,000 worth of gold, and has just found another rich deposit. Urn Rua is crushing regularly, and Attain!), with a floz, reef. Senma, with a 12ft reef, giving Lloz., Eridia, with five miles of reefs- over 30z.,fi1l look like making famous mines. This in five years, is a remarkable showing. In the whole desert, from co 2 miles south of Cairo to the Abyssinian frontier south of Khartourn—again to quote Mr. Alford—" the remains of ancient gold mines have been discovered," When these are opened up the net result will be prodigious. Many millons a year were turned out of Egyptian gold mines 2,ooo.years ago with no machinery ; what will be the amount to-day with all the modern appliances of an up-to-date mine ?

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR
NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. _Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith.

div.head: Social Service League.
div.p: The Social Service League.

Sir,—l notice that the lecture by Mrs. Cranston at Messrs. Crosfleld's Assembly Room on Monday has been reported to be under the auspices of the Social Service League. As the Secretary of this League, I wish to inform the public that this is wrong and that the Social -Service League has had nothing whatever to do with the matter. It has not been before the Committee of the League, nor did I, as Secretary, know anything at all about it, notwithstanding the fact that Mr. Dunnico stated that he was there as President of the Social Service League.—Your truly, JOHN MORTON, (Secretary Social Service League).

Rev. H. Duanico and Roman Catholics. Sir,—ln your issue of Saturday last, you gavei a report of my evidence before the magistrates at Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday the 10th inst. I am informed that such evidence has been mis-construed into an attack upon Roman Catholics. I desire to say that such an idea is erroneous. I differ as strongly from Roman Catholics on matters of dogma as Roman Catholics differ from me,but I have no desire to deprive them of what I claim for myself—freedom to worship God according to the dictates of conscience. On the occasion referred to I was permitted to use legal objections only hence my appeal to the Coronation Oath. Had I been allowed to say more I would have pointed out that I •have equally strong objections against State aid being given to any sectarian school. I stand by the principle that it is no part of the duty of the State to teach the dogmas of any sect. Tt ought to be possible for all sorts of Christian people to agree upon certain simple outlines of truth and morality being taught in the schools; if they cannot it is their reproach and disgrace. Anyhow, I have nothing but contempt for any Noncon- formist who avails himself of State aid to teach his own distinctive tenets. If the members of any religious body are not sufficiently impressed with the importance of their own beliefs to pay for the propagation of same —will let them perish.—Yours truly, HERBERT DUNNICO.

div.head: What Will the Voter do?
div.p: What Will the Voter do?

Sir,—" Higher Critic '• I observe is groping his way liken man in a fog, who fortunately through the action of the sun ultimately ends his way into the light. It is ftasy to perceive from his criticisms of my past letters that he is becoming somewhat doubtful about the wisdom of the Conservative party in introducing Chinese labour into South Africa, but like many others when they wish to make excuses for what they realise to be wrong ask," Well, wouldn't you have done just the same? " For " Higher Critic "in effect goes on to say " What are the Liberal party going to do when they get into office now that the Chinese are in South Africa ? " Well, singular to say, both Sir Edward Grey and Mr. Winston Churchill have during the past few days at the great meetings in Manchester answered that question by declaring that the Liberal party will get rid of the Chinese as soon as possible. How will it be done? Well. the Liberal Government will decline to renew the Ordinance which gave the mine owners power to introduce the Chinese, the result being that the Chinese will have to go back at the termination of their agreements. But the pity of this ugly South African business is that it has brought dishonour 'and discredit upon the fair fame of England throughout the world to say nothing of the £250,000,000 and 30,000 lives thrown away and the misery which has ensued. The South African war too, actually has swelled the ranks of the unemployed, for on the return of the soldiers of South Africa, many were unable to find work. Why the record of the Government, as the trnth gradually leaks out, is one of the worst of any that has ever sat at Westminster, especially when one takes into consider- ation the advantages of this supposed enlightened ago. Why it has just leaked out that this Government was actually proposing to plunge this country into a great war with Germany, over a very trumpery affair. I repeat that the more a man studies the history of his country and the record of Government, a working- man who votes for the Conservative Party is a "curiosity." Kind regards to "Higher Critic" and trusting he will further study and ponder over the Chinese Labour ques- tion in all its bearings, until his eyes are opened and his conscience pricked—fur voters are responsible as well as Governments.—l remain yours truly, FREE CRITIC.

div.head: Universal Training not Conscription.
div.p: Universal Training not Conscription.

Sir,--Tn your issue of October 14th jou vigorously applaud Lord Esher's backing up of the voluntary system and maintain that such a sentiment coming from so authoritative (?) a source will be a cold douche for the conscriptionists. I wonder if you have ever reflected that our present system of recruiting the regular army is conscription and that of the worst kind, for it is nothing more or less than a conscription of those who are unfit for the struggle of every day life. This is the result of our much vaunted love of freedom; the con- sequence of our selfish cry of" every man for himself." Of course I am not so innocent as to imagine that in repeating these glib phrases about conscription not solving our difficulties, you really believe that any one is proposing to compel men to serve abroad. No, it is only another instance of putting party before country. I No matter how important it may be that the people should not be led astray on this question, it is in your eyes still more important to seize hold of a good party cry. It is indeed only another instance of this lack of a national ideal which Matthew Arnold so eloquently deplored. What Lord Roberts and the members of the National Service League do propose is that each man should undergo a few months' training in a camp of exercise, so as to fit him to defend his country and to serve abroad 'voluntarily if the need should arise,jnst as men volunteered in the South African War, with the difference that they would know their job and not have to learn it at the expense of the lives of their comrades It is a matter of deep regret that a man of Lo r Esher's position should deal so superficially with se great a question. Any soldier will tell you that th minimum amount of training that will enable a citizen force to stand up against thoroughly disciplined troops is two or three months, and how are you on voluntary lines going to get volunteers to do that ? .The thing is absurd and ridiculous and the sooner we face facts and I give up talking drivel to the effect that " one volunteer is equal to ten pressed men" and the better. An American surgeon, who served in the war between the North and South, writing about the way in which the Germans and French fought in 1870 and the Russians and Japanese in 1904-5 says "the heroic fighting of the conscript soldiers of these nations has been far and away superior to the military qualities shown by the two millions of hired volunteers who fought for the Union against the South in 1861-65.—1 ant, yours &c., GEORGE CROSFIELD. Volunteer Quarters, Warrington, October 14th, 1905.

div.head: NOTES ON THE PROPERTY OWNERS'
div.p: NOTES ON THE PROPERTY OWNERS'
ASSOCIATION MEETING.
[By a Member.] The association gave evidence which has more than justified its birth and existence,

It is only three years old but it has already done good work not only among its own member, but also to the ratepayers of the town. It was through the efforts of some of its members that the time for payment of the paving of the streets was extended from three to seven years a " scheme " which has been beneficial to the ratepayer. There is now no excuse in delaying -the paving of streets and Warrington therefore made into a cleaner and healthier town by this means.

It has also shown by the attendance of its repre- sentatives at the Local Government Board Enquiries that it is taking a practical interest in the towns affairs and several Councillors have already borne testimony that undue expenditure in several Corpora- tion departments has been checked.

Mr. Councillor Burton gave some information which the ratepayers would be glad to hear. There was a strong possibility that the rates would be reduced next year. This is the result of more careful working on the part of the Town Council through pressure from outside.

The Property Owners Association also proved they were a diplomatic body and worked in the best interests of the whole of the town. They had no selfish aims, and realised that what was best for the inhabitants was also in the end to the interests of the Property Owners. Messrs. Hickman, Henshall, and England especially laid stress on these points • and showed that they wished to co-operate and assist the Corporation in its work.
Mete are now six Town Councillors members of die Association, five of whom have been elected on the Committee.

It will be noticed from the report of the apnnal meeting on Tuesday that intending candidates for the position of Town Councillors will be asked by the Association some "pertinent " questions, and will be supported or opposed according to the quality of their answers.

div.head: PROPERTY OWNERS' ASSOCIATION,
div.p: PROPERTY OWNERS' ASSOCIATION,
ANNUAL MEETING.
---- Criticism of Public Expenditure.

There was a good attendance at the annual meeting of the Warrington and District Property Owners' Association which was held in Tofts' Assembly Room, Bridge street, on Tuesday evening. Mr. R. flenshall (president) occupiod the chair and amongst those present were Councillors Pemberton, Lord, Burton and Evans, Messrs. W. Hickman, E. England, R. Dale, W. Winstanley, J. T. Whittle, W. Throssell, T. J. Hopkins (secretary). and R. Lunt (hon. treasurer).

div.head: REPORT.
div.p: THE REPORT.

The third annual report presented by the committee stated that the subscriptions received for the past twelve months amounted to £2O 7s. 6d. and the expendi- ture 13 7s. 10d., leaving a balance of £6 19s. Bd., which amount had been added to £6 18s. 8d brought forward from last year. The total in hand and in bank was £l3 18s. -Id. The Association held a public meeting, on sth December last, to consider the proposed extension of the Workhouse Infirmary, estimated to cost several thousand pounds, and sent letters requesting the Board of Guardians to re-consider the extension, the property owners considering the time inopportune owing to the increased assessments and present high rates. They were glad to report that the Guardiqns decided to postpone the building operations for twelve months. Repre- sentatives of the committee attended the Local Govern- ment Board Inquiries at the Town Hall, respecting the police buildings and electrical depot loans. The committee again appealed to all owners of property who had not already joined the association to become members, it having for its object the safe-guarding of their interests,which could only be attained by combina- tion. The association was non-political. It was gratifying to note an increased membership during the year of 32 making the total on register,lG3. On the motion of the PRESIDENT seconded by Mr. LCNT the report was adopted.

div.head: PRESIDENT.
div.p: THE PRESIDENT.

MR. HICKMAN AND PUBLIC EXPENDITURE. Mr. LUNT said the president had intimated that he found it somewhat difficult to fulfil the position and although he was willing to render them any assistance in his power, he would like to be released from the duties. He (Mr. Lunt) had therefore great pleasure in proposing a name which he thought would be accept- able to everyone—that of Mr. William Hickman who had done a good work for the association. He had acted for twelve months as chairman of the committee and would no doubt -nake a very energetic and able president. (Applause.) Mr. R. DALE seconded and the motion was unani- mously agreed to. In returning thanks Mr Mi.:Kayo; said that when he joined the Association it was the farthest thought from his mind to take an official position. As they had done him the honour of electing him unanimously he would endeavour to do his best for the interests of the Association which he believed was worthy of the sup- port of every member and of every property owner in Warrington and district. They were not an association of "stick in the muds,"neither were they an association of agitators nor of obstructionists, but he believed they were willing to co-operate with "the powers that be" for the best interests of the town. He was very pleased with the progress the Association had already made. When they considered that in so short a time the membership had grown to 163,a1l being property owners who had something at stake, and were also interested in the town as citizens, it appeared that the prospects were very encouraging. The Association was only in its infancy, and it took some time to let the public know its possibilities. He thought that in the future the Association should be able to do inure work than it had accomplished in the past. He did not see why during the next year the membership should not be doubled. They had already, he thought, done something to check the heavy expenditure in the town. In Warrington there had been too ranch rushing with regard to public buildings. (Applause). Great buildings had been erected which might have waited for a time. (Hear, hear). He concurred with the remarks , of a gentleman who told him that Warrington wanted to rest a while so that things might recover themselves.' They wanted five years rest and unless it was absolutely necessary no public building should be erected for the present. It would, he thought,l be to the benefit of the town generally to keep back expenditure on buildings as long as , possible. The" powers that be" might go more care- fully into the question of whether they could reduce the rates a little. (Applause.) There was a very great demand for money by the Town Council, Board of Guardisns,and Education Committee.but if those bodies I could unite to keep expensive schemes back as long as Possible and reduce the rates it would be a great advantage and would benefit the workingmen for the rents would he reduced accordingly. The manufacturers —some of whom had bad a very struggling time— would also feel the advantage. If we were to induce other manufacturers to come to the town! we must endeavour to keep the rates as low as possible. He took it that the Association was not formed to dictate to the Town Council, Board of Guardians, or anyone else, but to co-operate with them. If there was anything about the town which needed improving or any scheme that ought to be deferred, they as rate- payers and property owners had a right to raise their voices and enter a protest or offer advice. He might inform the meeting that there was likely to be a change with regard to the assessments. He had supported such a change in the Assessment Committee for some years. There had certainly been inequalities, and the Committee and Assistant Overseer had been trying to devise a scheme whereby tbeassessments might be more equitable all over the borough. The Committee wanted to apply it to the borough alone, but he strongly con- tended that it should also cover the parts of the Union outside Warrington. It might make a little difference to some people, but on the whole he thought it would he a good thing, and an honest and equitable measure by which the town generally NE,ould benefit. The Association was only asking for justice and was not begging for favours. There had been some inequalities in the town which had not been very creditable to them but in future they would endeavour as an association to see that everyone bore their fair share of local taxation. (Applause).
RETIRING PRESIDENT AND THE ASSOCIATION'S POLICY.

On the motion of Councillor PEMBERTON seconded by Mr. ENG LAND, a vote of thanks was accorded to the retiring president. Mr. HENSIIALL, in acknowledging the compliment,said he had taken a very deep interest in the work of the Association' as he was increasingly convinced that there was work for an association of that character if it were wisely guided and had right ideals. Every year,with- out encouraging a policy of decentralization, power was being given to local authorities such as even the ardent reformers of fifty years ago never dreamed of. To bear some humble part in the right governing of one's town was therefore a right ideal. The Association's policy was not one of "cheap and nasty." It was not a ques- tion of low rates at any price. The ideal he had set before the Association last year was that the rate which I they should try to keep lower than any other was the death rate. If for the fuller development of the town I expenditure on health and educational matters and other I essentials were necessary he was prepared to pay it. I The Association should keep before it the ideal of pure and efficient government and strive to realize civic righteousness. Their policy should be one of construc- tive criticism. I THE ECONOMY OF THE ASSOCIATION.

Councillor BURTON remarked that if the Corporation were only half as economical as the Association had been in conducting their business the rates would per- haps go down about 50 par cent. Mr. ENGLAND in supporting the election of Councillox Lord to the committee said he would like to see almost the whole of the councillors as members of the assocci- ation. One of the aims of the organization was really to co-operate with and,if possible,help the Corporation They had no special axe to grind. Whatever their views might be on the question of non-trading—and some of them might think it had been done a little bit too much—they felt that Councillor Lord was honest and genuine and would serve the association well. Eventually the following were elected as the com- mittee: Councillors Burton, Barton, Lord, Evans, Pem- berton and Skelland • Metsrs. It. ilenshall,W. Throssell, Lee IL Thornton, Longshaw, H. Winstanley, J. T. IVlafttle, It. Dale, W.H. Stansfield,W. Winstanley,Diggle, J.T. Barton and Cooper. THE TREASURER.

Oa the motion wqr7liiiirriCE.,-;onded by Mr. R DALE, Mr. Lunt was re-elected treasurer and cordially thanked for his past services. In returning thanks Mr. Luyr said he would not be content until they had two-thirds of the property- owners members of the association.
THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. fit:a GESTED APPROACHING OF CANDIDATE.

The SECRETARY mad a letter from Mr. H.J.Longton, in which he said " ['ho association is to be heartily congratulated upon the result of its efforts during the past year,particularly in connection with its opposition ta the proposed unnecessary extention of the Workhouse Infirmary. I think the solicitor of the association should be instructed to attend and watch, on behalf of the association, all public inquiries with regard to the borrowing of ratepayers' money, and if he were in- stnicted beforehand he would be able to prepare him- self for those occasions. I also venture to suggest that the candidates for the municipal elections should be interviewed on behalf of the association, and that they should be supported or opposed according to whether or not they are in favour or opposed to our objects ; and, if necessary, that we should run our own I candidates." - - - - _
A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Longton for the interest he has taken in the work of the Associa- tion. Speaking in support Councillor PE3IBERTON said the

div.head: Examiner, saturday, October 21, 1905.
div.p: The Examiner, saturday, October 21, 1905.

property owners ought to bestir themselves and they would carry great weight with the authorities. They would be able to secure benefitsnot only for themselves but also for the working classes. Mr, S, Goumt was of the opinion that the Associa- tion ought to have a direct representative on the Town Council.

The Cil NIRMAN said that they hoped that during the corning year a great many Councillors Ivho were property owners would join the Association. Councillor PEM BERTON suggested that questions should be put to the candidates at the forthcoming elections. _ _ _

Councillor BURTON said the Association had already had weight not only upon the Corporation and Board of Guardians but in other directions. The Corporation and Guardians had been more careful in spending the ratepayers' money and the result was that last year they had a small reduction in the Borough rates. He thought there was little doubt that they would have another reduction next year. With those facts before them, it would be well not to run a candidate of their own. It might introduce a little political feeling amongst them and in the end do them more harm than good. The CHAIRMAN questioned whether the Association would accomplish a great deal by running its own candidates. At present six members of the Town Council were members of the Association and five were members of the committee. Councillor EVANS said the Town Council bad never had from the Association such influence brought to bear as was exercised on the Board of Guardians. The committee of the Association ought to keep an over- sight of the expenditure and when necessary ask the members of the Council who were connected with the Association to raise any questions of importance. He was of the opinion that the Education Committee could be worked—and efficiently worked—with a saving of perhaps thousands of pounds a year. (Applause.) The work could be divided into sectionsginstead of practic- ally everything being left in the hands of one general committee—the School Management Committee. The authority ought to be brought into more direct touch with the school managers. Under the present condi- tions the committee might possibly be paying £7O a year to a teacher when £5O or £6O would do. Councillor LORD proposed that a committee should meet to formulate questions to be put to candidates for the Town Council. The Association should also con- sider the question of street paving for, he contended, the way streets were put down in many instances had been scandalous. The Association should take that matter up because he felt it would be the means of saving hundreds and perhaps thousands of pounds. Several members endorsed these remarks. Councillor PEMBERTON seconded Councillor Lord's resolution and it was carried. It was also decided that the committee should take steps at the commencement of the new year to obtain the affiliation of the Association with the United Property Owners' and Ratepayers' Association of Great Britain.

inspectors round who would more or less find fault with what they were doing. That was not at all the spirit of the committee. Physical instruction was for the first time made a compulsory subject in every school and consequently it was the duty of the School Manage- ment Committee and not of the Gymnasium Committee to see that the subject was properly taught in every school in the town. The committee was in this posi- tion. They had a number of teachers who were perfectly qualified to give physical instruction and a smaller but appreciable number who were not so qualified. It therefore seemed to the committee that it was advisable to provide for those teachers with some assistance which would qualify them to give physical instruction. They had arranged to do that and had also arranged that classes should be held at the Gymnasium for those teachers who desired to qualify themselves. Ile gymnasium inspector would visit the school and act as a friendly advisor. (Hear, hear.) If he went to a school and saw the teacher giving drill well and everything going on right then his duty ended but if he found a teacher who was not giving the instruction in the best possible way he, would, at the conclusion of the class, interview the teacher and point out anything which would enable him to improve his teaching. He wished to make it perfectly clear that they did not desire to subject the teachers in any way to unnecessary interference or to an inspection which would prove distasteful. In the first place the inspector would be under the direction and control of the School Management Committee and if it was found that dissatisfaction was caused amongst the teachers by the way in which he discharged his duties, though he did not for a moment anticipate that would happen, the committee could complain to the Gymnasium Committee. The whole scheme was of a temporary character and at the end of twelve months it would be competent for them to say that the teachers were entirely qualified to undertake physical instruction without any extraneous help whatever, and the services of the gymnastic inspector would no longer be required. The Rev. FATHER WILSON seconded.

The Rev. JOHN YONGE asked whether any representa- tion had been made to the managers of the Warrington British School with regard to an objection to the terms of the scheme ? He understood that the managers of that school objected, from manifest and practical reasons to the instructing of the children at the Gymnasium. Alderman BENNETT : A letter has been received but it has not yet been before the committee. The Rev. JOHN YONGE thought that as the managers of the school bad a very serious objection tho minute should be referred back until the objection had been before the committee.

The director read the letter from the managers of the Warrington British School, in which they expressed their objection to the proposals of the committee on the ground that the taking of the children to the Gymnasium would seriously interfere with the working 'of the school and that it was better to continuo the present system of giving the instructions in the school play-.round. Alderman BENS ETT thought it better to take the re- port as it stood and deal with the objection later on on its merits. He thought it would cause delay to send the whole of the report back. The Bev. JOHN YONGE moved that the portion of the minute relating to the sending of the children to the Gymnasium be referred back. Mr. TINS WORTH moved the referring back of the 'whole of the minute. When the matter was first broaght 'forward the arrangement which had been come to did not commend itself to the School Management Corn- ! mittee. The question of taking the children from the Warrington British School to the Gymnasium was one of the principal questions in the whole matter. It came as a surprise to him to know that there was an objection on the part of the managers to that being done. They were paying L'loo a year for the use of the Gymnasium for that purpose, and if the children were not taken the money would be wasted. Alderman BENNETT pointed out that the referring beck of the minute would disorganize the whole of their arrangements, as the new system should come into opera tion on the Ist November.
The Rev. JOHN YoNui seconld Mr. Unsworth's amendment.

Alderman PIERPOINT suggested that the dilficulty could be met by the alteration of the text end by the replacing of the word "shall" by "may." Hr. HENRY ROBERTS thought the suggestion an admirable one and one which mot every practical diffi- culty. As one who had taken a leading part in effecting the settlement, he hoped the committee would not throw their work to the winds. They thought the managers of People's College were anxious to go to the gymnasium but they would certainly not be forced to go if they did not want to. If any other arrangement could be made which would satisfy the committee they would be only too pleased to fall in with it. The constant referring back of minutes to those who had given their time and ability in trying to elucidate the various points was calculated to reflect upon the dignity of the committee. Alderman BENNETT : Alderman Pierpoint's sugges- tion cannot be adopted as it is not in accerdance with the Standing Orders. Mr. Ronmrs :—Standing Orders be blowed ! There are too many of them. The MAYOR urged that there need not be so much discussion as to one committee paying more to another committee than it ought to do. The money all came out of the rates and was just the same no matter whether it was taken out of the left pocket or the right pocket. The Education Co =ate° were fully entitled to use the Gymnasium. . .

Mr. UrsoN said that so far as he had been able to ascertain the teachers were almost unanimous against the scheme, but be thought if they could have heard Canon Stevenson's statement their objections would have been removed. A wrong impression had arisen with regard to the monthly reports by the inspectors of their visits to the school, as there was an idea that the reports would be either of approve' or condemna- tion and would perhaps materially affect the positions of the teachers.

N-fr.-13-rIN---sTo-x- thought the letter from the managers of the Warrington British School should be considered and the committee should not lose sight of the fact that the large majority of the teachers were qualified to give physical instruction without interfemnce or super- vision from the instructors at the gymnasium. Mr. MAY: How can we ascertain the competency of the teachers 'unless the inspector goes round and pre- smts a;report? Canon STevENsox thought the minutes could be passed without any difficulty being in Any way created. The letter from the managers of the Warrington British School had not been before the committee who wore under the impression that they desired that the children from the school should be drilled at the gyrnnasium,and believed they wore consulting tho interests of the managers in making those arrangements. The arrange- ment would not be forced upon them if they did not want it. He read the resolution to mean that the scholars should use the gymnasium if desired and he thought that was how all sensible persons would read it. (Laughter). The force was not imperative but permissive. If the minutes were not passed they would be inn very serious difficulty as they had made the arrangements for com- mencing the new system on November Ist. The reports which would be presented by the inspector would not in any way be inquisitorial. Mr. UNSWORTII said the letter of protest was the principal course of his moving the amendment which after hearing the statement by Canon Stevenson, he would withdraw. . _

The Rev. JOITN YONGE consented to the withdrawing of the amendment. He could not, he said, help think- ing however that if the students in the institution over which Canon stevenson so admirably presided placed the same construction upon words as the Canon and construed "shall" to mean "you may if you like," Canon Stevenson would find himself in a difficult posi- tion. (Laughter.) SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMAITTEE.

EXCLUSION OF INFANTS. THE DUTY OF THE EDUCATION CONINIITITE. The adoption of the minutes of the School Attend- ance Committee was moved by Councillor Ellison and seconded be Councillor Barton. C mon 'STE VEXsON referred to a resolution to exclude children under the age of five years , from attendance at. the Latchford school, and St. George's schools. He would like the Cnairman of i the Committee to give a little more information. He quite recognized that in certain schools which were overcrowded it would be an advantage to exclude young children as it would give greater accommodation. The whole question was a very serious one. He quite agreed that between the ages of three and five years a child should have practically no intellectual training so far as teaching went. If, however, they excluded children under the ages of five years whose homes were not good the effect upon thoso children would be extremely serious both morally and physically. In cases where the mother had to go out to work the children would be turned into the streets. If the Committee were going to provide crachee for the children he would.welcome the approval with both hands. Mr. MAY said he would like to call attention to the weighty and serious words which fell from a former Warrington schoolmaster at a recent dinner. Mr. Dew- hurst, to whom hs referred, said the Committee would be making a great mistake if they excluded children between the ages of three and five years, as the teachers would never be able to make up what the child lost, and the general standard of education would fall. Alderman SMETIIURST thought that if it was sur- rounded by a good home influence it was imperative that it should be brought up at home.. He thought that on the ground of health young children should not be permitted to attend school. Some parents thought of nothing except bringing children into the world, and then left the world to look after the children. Colonel Bucivrox said the Education Committee existed for the purpose of educating children, and not nursing them. Children perhaps did require nurses, but it was not the duty of the Education Committee to provide nurses. Ile took it they did not mean to exclude all children who were not five. Children however, were sent to school when they were too young to fix their attention upon anything for any length of time. The question of mothers going to work and the children being on the streets applied after school hours as well. It was all nonsense to suggest that the Education Committee must take upon them- selves the duties of nurse to those children. Where they I had accommodation and desired to fill the school young
children wOuld not be excluded as they would be from schools which were overcrowded. _

Mr. PLlNurox pointed out that the Committee had been called upon by managers of the schools to take that question into consideration with the result that in certain schools children under the age of five years would not be received. The exclusion was not on the broad lines suggested by several speakers. Mr. H. ROBERTS said he was glad to learn that was the case as although CanoniStevenson had only mentioned one side there was an additional side to be discussed when they came to consider the broad question. It was all very well •to say it was not their duty to promote accommodation for children under the lage of five years, but they had to consider the interests of the children, and to see to their up bringing and then moral and physical development. That duty was gradually devolving upon education committees as they happened to tie the only public bodies who had control of the children for any length of time. Public sentiment demanded that the interest of the children should be looked to first and that the children should not suffer through the neglect of the parents. The interests of the children were par- amount and any little expenditure which might be in- curred would be entirely wiped out in two generations by the improved stamp of the children of the future. Although he quite agreed that we should not take parents responsibility on our own shoulders and ad- mitted that a considerable proportion of parents were unmindful of their responsibilities, he thought it would pay the State to take over those responsibilities, for a single generation in consideration of the improvement we should got in the physical and moral status of the children. (Hear, hear.) However, when they came to deal with the question generally they must look it it all round, and see that the interests of the children were not neglected. Councillor EcusoN replied to the discussion, and said the present arrangement was only a temporary one applying to St. George's and Latchford Council Infants' School which were overcrowded. No doubt when more accommodation was provided the whole matter would be considered and put on a proper basis. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were approved. THE NEW SCHOOL. _

THE EXCLUSION 9F INFANTS FROM SCHOOL. ---- Physical Instruction.
THE FUTURE OF THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL.

The monthly meeting of this committee was held on Monday evening, at the Town Hall,under the presidency of Alderman Bennett. There were also present, Alder- man Pierpoint (deputy-chairman).Alderman Bolton and Smethurst, Councillors Barton, Craik, Ellison, Evans, Lord, Sankey, Fulton Smith, Wright and Wilkinson, Messrs. IV. Bibby,J. D. Buckton,A. J,Jolley,H. Kingdon, T. May, C. E. Parker, E. Plinston, H. Roberts, Rev. Canon Stevenson, Messrs. C. H. Unsworth, J. Upson, G. Walker, N. Wilson, .1. Yonge, and Mr. J. Moore Murray (director), Mr. John Fairhurst (treasurer). FINANCE COMMITTEE.

div.head: COMPARATIVE STATEMENT ASKED FOR.
div.p: COMPARATIVE STATEMENT ASKED FOR.
Mr. A. J, JOLLEY moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Finance Committee.

Colonel BUCKTON seconded. Mr. MAY said he had to make his usual protest and be begged to call attention to minute B 322 which read :--" A comparative statement of the receipts and expenditure ot the committee during the half-year ended the 30th September, 1903, with the estimates for the whole of the year was submitted and noted." That statement was of public interest and importance to the members of the Education Committee and it seemed strange that not the slightest further notice was taken of it. It would be interesting to know how much the cost of education had increased during the past half-year. Speaking for himself he was entirely in the dark, and he had not the slightest idea whether the cost of education had increased or decreased. The , minutes of the Town Council contained comparative statements. For instance,it was reported that the total income from the markets was £485 and for the corres- ponding period last year £149, or an increase of £35. The CHA IRMAN : That is at the end of the year. Mr. MAY No, it is a monthly statement. Continu- ing, Mr. May said he had had nearly 40 years' experi- ence of income and expenditure with regard to the country, and the comparative statements were of great use to the public at large ; almost in fact, to the world at large. In his own case he had never made a state- ment to the Government without submitting a compare for the preceding period, month or year. It was a check upon him and upon the person paying the money, and useful information to the public. It had several advantages and he thought the Education Committee ought to follow the example of the Town Council. The CHAIRMAN : There is no such general rule of the Council. In the case of one or two of the com- mittees, where there are trading concerns, an exception is made, but not in regard to the whole of the com- mittees. Whilst a comparative statement is supplied to the responsible committee it is not published ? it is sufficient, I think, to supply it to the responsible com- mittee.

_ Mr. MAY then moved as an amendment that the minute in question be referred back for tho introduction of the compare. The amendment was not seconded. Mr. A. J. Jor..r.Ev stated for the information of all present that there was not the smallest desire to sup- press anything. The information asked for would be supplied to anyone who asked for it ,it was before him. Sometimes the committee were blamed for wasting printers' ink in circulating unnecessary particulars, and now they were blamed for not doing so. Alderman SmErmmtsz : Would you simply state what is the difference, and then we should all under- stand?

Mr. JOLTAW : We have not got the figures of the expenditure of this year compared with the expenditure of last year, but if Mr- May had r.sad the minutes he would have seen they give a comparison of the actual receipts with the estimated receipts and expenditure. Mr. RonEwrs said this was not a comp trative state- ment in the sense Mr. May suggested. It was a com- parison between the estimates of the year and the actual income and expenditure of the year. It was not a comparison of the receipts and expenditnre of this year with the receipts and expenditure of the previous year. The minutes were approved. THE FUTURE OF TIM GRAMMAR SCHOOL. PHYSICAL INSTRUCTION.

_ - The School Management C.) ninitteo submitted a scheme for the physical instruction of children. The Director reported the receipt of the following letter : —" Dear Sir,—At a representative meeting of the Warrington Head Teacher's Association, held on Friday, the 13th inst., it was unanimously resolved that the following representation bo nude to the Education Committee ou the question of the appointment of an inspector to visit and report on the physical exercises taught in the schools of the county borough,' We, the head teachers of this town, are of opinion that the appointment of a drill inspector is unnecessary and mischievous on the following grounds. It is mischiev- ous because outside interference with the responsibili- ties of the head teachers is to be deprecated and is likely to lead to friction. It is unnecessary because 1(1) The majority of the teachors hold drill certificates and are consequently fully competent to te.ch this subject. (2) 'rho physical exercises are now being satisfactorily taught in all the schools. (3) No adverse report has yet been presented by H.M. Inspectors, who are specially qualified to judge the character of the instruction given.' We would, therefore, most respect- fully suggest that the appointment be not confirmed. I am to ask you to be good enough to bring this repre- sentation before the next meeting of the Education !Committee.—Believe 1119, yours truly, J. W. PARKER, ! hon. secrettry. To the Secretary of the Education Committee." , . .

Canon Monf,Ev STEVEZ,NON moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Committee with the exception of the minutes referring to the conference between the committee and the Governors of the Grammar school. The School Management Committee had held a very important conference with the Governors of the Grammar school upon certain points in the amended scheme, but, unfortunately, from want of time they had been unable to finish conference which had been adjourned. He had every hope that when they met again they would be able not only to finish it, but to come to a substantial agreement between the two bodies,That being the ease he thought it would be in- advisable for them to debate in public the points upon which they had conferred privately and he therefore ventured to ask the committee to postpone for a month that discussion which must enevitably take place and which owing to the importance of the subject certainly ought to take place. An adjournment of the discussion would enable them to thoroughly study the question. The committee had hold another conference With the Gymnasium Committee and had come to an agreement which he hoped would be satisfactory. He regretted that the scheme did not commend titself to the headmasters of the town but he ventured to think that when they became acquainted with the spirit which animated the committee their objections would be greatly minimised if not entirely removed. There seemed to be an impression in the minds of some of the teachers that there was a desire to unnecessarily interfere with their work as teachers and to send

div.head: E §7I`S7IEXCEEDED.
div.p: E §7I`S7IEXCEEDED.

The committee reported the receipt of a notification I from the Board of Education approving of the plans for the erection of the "Bolton' Council school as pro- viding accommodation for not more than 360 girls and 360 infants, and for a cookery centre for 18 scholars at practice and 54 at demonstration. They resolved that the architect for the erection of the Council school be instructed to prepare the necessary detailed specifica- tion, the working drawings, and the bills of quantities, and to submit the same to the Surveyor and the Director for their approval; and that, when the same have been approved the necessary advertisement be issued inviting tenders for the erection of the school in accordance therewith. The sub-committee also resolved that the tender of Mr. C. W. Davenport, amounting to I £13,784 10s. for the erection of the "Beamotat " Council school be accepted; that application be made to the Board lof Education for their sanction to the raising of a loan to cover the cost of the erection and furnishing of the building ; that no deviation from nor alteration of the ' plans, specification and bills of quantities be permitted 'without the written consent of this committee, and that an advertisement be issued inviting applications for the post of clerk of works for both the Beamont " and Bolton" Council schools, at an inclusive salary at the rate of £3 10s. per week. The Mayon, in proposing the confirmation of the above minutes, said it would he seen that they had at last got sanction to go on with the Bolton school, and they were doing their best to carry out the work. They had accepted the tender for the work, and they asked for that to be now confirmed. The amount was con- siderably more than the sum, which had been exceeded, with other items, by something like 25 per cent., but the Borough Surveyor assured them that it was impos- sible to get the work done for the sum they expected at first.

Alderman SMETHURST seconded the motion. Councillor LORD asked what other tenders had been received and if tho lowest tenders had been accepted. Mr. MAI.' said he griked what amount per head the cost amounted to. The CHAIRMLIN : .Cl 2 83: Dd.
Mr. MAY : It was stated last week by the Chairman of the Architects' Association in Manchester that the cost there was from £7 10s. to £lO.

The MAYOR : That man was off it altogether— (laughter)—because we went through a whore list of schools in various towns, including Manchester, Liver- pool and Birkenhead and in no case did we find one at £lO per head. Therefore, the architect you refer to was alluding to the foundation and forgetting the structure. (Laughter.) Continuing, he said with reference to Councillor Lord's question he might say that there were thirteen tenders ranging from £13,000 odd to the amount of Hr. Davenport's tender, which was the loweet, and the one accepted. There seemed to be a general idea that they had something to cloak and to hicte, and if that was the case the sooner they had the fullest information the better. His Worship then proceeded to read the amounts of the various tenders to show that the lowest had been accepted. The minutes were approved. SECONDARY SCHOOL MATRON. MR. PLINSTON'S MOTION A BREEZE.

Mr. E. PLINSTON had given notice to move: "(1), That the public and press be excluded from this meeting of the Education Committee at this stage of the pro- ceedings ; (2), that the resolution of the 'Education Committee at their meeting on the 28th August, 1905, appointing Miss Elizabeth Frost senior assistant mistress at the Secondary School,be rescinded,and(3)that the School Management Sub-committee be instructed tore-consider the appointinfMt."

. • Mr. PLINSTON formally moved the first resolution stating as his reason for doing so that personalities might arise during the discussion which it wiz desirable should be kept private. Councillor LORD seconded.

Mr. FIENnv ROBERTS: Why should the press be ex- cluded ? It is rather curious that a member of a party which is continually crying for more light should wish a matter of this importance to be discussed in camera: I protest very strongly against • the exclusion of the press and hope the committee will not pass the resolution.

Mr. PLINATON : Will you allow Me to explain? The CIIAIRmAN- : I think the reason is pretty obvious, and I think there was a feeling at the last meeting that the question should not be discussed in public as personalities might arise. The MAYOR: There has been no reason given why this question should be discussed in camera. If it is a matter for a committee it should be brought before a committee. If it is something we want light upon let it go before an investigation committee which they are so fond of having. Personally I don't want to have anything to do with a thing which cannot be dis- cussed in public. Mr. PARKER said he thought they had confidence in the members of the Press, and they could leave it to them to leave out any personal matter which might be introduced.

The MArou : They will do that all right. Mr. PARKER : There may arise during the discus- sion something which might reflect upon the persons! cnaracter of the candidates which it is not desirable should be made public. Councillor LORD said that was his only reason for seconding the motion. He had no desire for any dark- ness and was only too pleased to have anything made public. It was only out of respect for the feelings of the ladies concerned that he suggessed not discussing it in public. Alderman BENNETT : That is my feeling. Ur. RonEnTs : I would like it to be understood, Mr. Chairman, that that is your private opinion alone, because it is not my opinion at all. •The CHAIRMAN : That, of course, is my own opinion. I speak for myself only. Mr. ROBERTS : I don't accept that explanation. T absolutely decline to believe in any one coming here and protesting against the admission of the Press, whose whole public life has been a contradiction of such a course. _ _
Mr. PraNsTos : May I make my meaning clear? Mr. ROBERTS : lam not referrin,, to you.

Councillor LORD : !leis referring—to Me. Mr. ROBERTS: I refer to the gentleman next to you. , who has had the audacity, in the light of his own con- duct, to second the motion. ; Councillor Luttp : I don't withdraw from my position at all. ; The motion was then put to the meeting and defeated. Mr. VLINSTON, in moving his resolution, said his ' reason for doing so was merely: to get to know the reasons why a teacher who was junior to two others should be appointed the matron of the school. Councillor LOCLD seconded. Canon STEVENSON said he greatly regretted being absent from the last meeting, but he could explain the matter now. He could assure Mr. Plinston there was nothing in the matter which reflected on the personal character of any of the ladies concerned in any way. (Hear, hear.) The committee had been actuated solely by the desire to appoint the person best suited for the post, and they had made the selections which, in their opinion, was the best. He must admit there had been some confusion on this matter, but he did not think any , particular one was to blame. There had, as the mem- bers knew, been changes at the Technical School, and between the time Mr. Gow left and the time of 'Mr. Itobson's coming there seemed to have been some con- fusion as to the duties of the lady occupying the post of matron. So far as they could discover the duties had been fulfilled by the lady the committee had chosen' ; from the time of Mr. Gow and,therefore,although in one sense the appointment was a new one, the lady was merely carrying out the duty she performed unofficially from the start. To go back now and make a change would be very inadvisable unless there was some grave reason for it, and he thought it much the best thing to allow it to rest. (Hear, hear.) Thera was nothing to hide in any way. Mr. JOLLEY endorsed the Canon's statement. Mr. PLINSTON said he was exceedingly obliged to Canon Stevenson for his explanation, and only wished to say that if he and other members had been as i courteously and civilly treated n the past as they had that night by the Canon, this matter would not have gone as far as it had. (Hear, hear.) He was perfectly satisfied and withdrew his motions with their permission. d The subject then closed.

Marriage at Stockton Heath. The marriage was solemized at St. Thomas' Church on Tuesday afternoon of Miss Lillian Maude Sutton, of Ivy Done, • Stockton Heath, and Mr. Harold Hollows, of Legh and Bedford. Considerable interest was taken in the event and there was a large attendance at church. The officiating cleryman was the Rev. H. V. Pigot. The bride wore a dress of white eolienne silk, trimmed with Brussells lace: and carried a shower bouquet of 'white liles and maidenhair fern, the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids were Miss Maggio Sutton and Miss Daisy Hayes, who wore dresses of pale pink eolienne silk, trimmed with real Irish lace, and pink satin ribbons, and carried shower bouquets of 7ellow chrysanthemums, maidenhair fern and white satin streamers. The best man was Mr. Percy Gornall, of Leigh and Bedford. The reception was held the Winmarleigh Cafe. Many beantiful presents were receired.

div.head: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
Election of President.

There was a large attendance of members at the quarterly meeting of the Warrington Co-operative Society, which was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Monday evening. Mr. T. CritchleYr president-elect, occupied the chair. THE LATE MR. W. JEFFERY. The following report, which was submitted by the Committee, was approved :—Your Committee have to express their deep sorrow in recording the death of our esteemed president, Mr. William Jeffery. His appoint ment to the office of President took place at the last half-yearly meeting, on July 17th, which was the first and last meeting which he attended as President. He served on the Committee of Management for 25 years- which shows a long record of service in the history of the Society. PROGRESS OF THE SOCIETY. Mr. CRITCHLEY said their sales for the past quarter amounted to £35,654, an increase of £1,807 upon the corresponding quarter of last year. He would like to draw their attention to tho progress the Society had made since they started their branch which was opened at Stockton Heath on July 19, 1902—three years ago.,' Since the opening of that branch, there had been alai increase in the sales per quarter of £6,500 and dividends of £1,190 in three years. (Applause.) They- had 6,500 members at the end of 1902, and now thet,, had about 7,800. (Applause.) BEAUTIFUL WARRINGTON. The Committee recommended the granting of the use; of the Co-operative Hall free to the Committee of the Beautiful Warrington Society provided that the objecte; of the Society were carried out. DONATIONS TO THE NURSING ASSOCIATIO.I -- The PRESIDENT said the committee recommended that £5O be given to the 'Warrington and District Nurs-. ing Association. This was because of a letter received from Mr. F. Monks, which stated that the Institution:, was now £149 16s. 6d. in debt. Mr. Monks pointed out that many members of the Society were receiving assist- ance from the Association. Mr. GEORGE WALLINGTON said he was a subscriber to the Nurses' Association,and he knew that Mr. Monks had assisted it a great deal out of his own pocket. He felt prepared to backup the committee, and though as they had been giving money freely of late, they could, never give it to a more deserving object than the Nurses Association. The/ should do anything which would encourage the Institution in their good work, and he - moved that the Society subscribe not £5O but £lOO. Mr. CROWTHER : Has the Society been a subscriber in the past ? The SECRETARY : Yes. We first subscribed £5

year, but we found so much good was being done and Sol little response was made to the appeals, especially by ' the rich people, that we were told it had become : necessary that a larger subscription should be made, s 0 o"!; we doubled our subscription and are now paying £lO., 'Apfor.ik e.t,R .t. l‘cr. Monks,ol\h,as spent hundreds of pounds out of his own, objected to Mr. Wallington's motion. Its t thought they were getting too lavish, and • they were giving too much away to one object. He granted that the Association was 5 , very good one and one worthy of support but they were already subscribing well to it and many meni'j hers themselves were doing so. If there were snch an., amount of money to be given away, he would iike, them to look nearer home and give something among' their own deserving people. There were men working in connection with the Society ever since it started, whom they should look to. They should not give so IL much money to outside objects, and he moved that the minute of the committee authorising the donation 01 £:;0 la confirmed.

There was no seconder to Mr. Wallington's resolutlee which fell to the ground and the proposal of the coal' induce was approved. APPLICATION OF' STOCK VALUER. Hr. Lowk asked how it was that Mr. Critchley being; i a member of the committee had also been appointed . stock valuer. He contended thataccording to the rola • no one who was a paid servant was entitled to be ou the committee.

Mr. N. CooK presumed that the committee had a feet right to nominate the stock valuer;and he coula not see any reason why Mr. Critchley could not bola the position until the annual meeting. The PRESIDENT explained that since the death of Mt.., Bircball he had performed the duties of stock valuer, and as he had been re-appointed the last quarter be pre- sumed he had performed the duties satisfactorily. Mr. HMEERT said they had had a precedent of 20 years for the present arrangement,and it had acted well., Mr. Low 6 contended they should stick to the rule* and he wanted to know where the line was going to be drawn if they commenced breaking the rules. The Secretary said that when Mr. Rathbone wa,.° appointed secretary and manager it was arranged thau Mr. Birchall be appointed to take the stock into con' sideration, and to put his own value upon it. Th appointment was made so that no suspicion whatever . should rest upon Mr. Rathbone as manager and 96.0'0" tary. Mr. Birchall performed those duties to the time of his death, since which time Mr. Critchley had don, the work. He wanted to know where they were going to get an outside man who could do the work. The matter then dropped, it being understood t 113., Mr. Lowe would bring it up at the annual meeting. ' ' ELECTION OF PRESIDENT. 1 , • It was decided unanimously, on the motion of Mr. -"‘" FARRAR, seconded by Mr. J. OWEN, that Mr. Critchlet be president of the Fiociety until the annual meeting-- The newly elected PRESIDENT thanked the member.A and promised to do all he could to help and to benefit' ' the Society. He was quite willing to bestow ail amount of time for the benefit of the SocietY• ELECTION OF COMMITTEE MAN. One committeeman was required in the place of /kit' Critchley who was elected president, and there Were six candidates for the Position: Messrs. Rushton, Lo..,w,eL, J. Owen, W. Haigh, N. Cook and 11. Emerson. 1-"` : first voting by ballot resulted as follows :—Cook, 21 - Rushton, 20; Lowe, 13; Haigh, 12; Owen, 11; Emerson, 6. As Mr. Cook had not an absolute majority, t. 113 three highest names were-put to the meeting again vilt the following result :—Caok, 43 ; Rushton, 25 ; Lo% 19. As Mr. Cook was only one short of au absolut majority, it was decided by a show of hands that he be elected to the vacant position. PROPOSAL TO NAME THE CO-OPERATIVE

div.head: _BUILDINGS.
div.p: _BUILDINGS.

Mr. Tnow thougict—s.;;;thing—should be done perpetuate the memory of old Co-operators,ani better could be chosen than by naming the buildingS•:' Thus there could be the " Rathbone buildings," the'i "Jeffery buildiqgs," the " Robert Cook buildings," He was sure that this would do much toward keepinsl the memory of those old members green. Mr.FARRErt thought this was a question which mig,lit, be referred to the committee. There were, he remind Mr. Trow, photographs being placed in the CO mittee room, and this would keep old co-operators 10 the memory of future generations. ChTERILL Supported) Mr. Troves suggestions. Mr. Tnow said he had never been in the committev room in his life and he was sure that photographs would not be seen by the general public. The matter dropped and the meeting terminated.

lOUNTi BOROUGH OF WARRINGTOS NJ MUNICIPAL ELECTION. NOVEMBER 18'r., 1905. TO THE ELECTORS OF HOWLEY WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, Having been requested by the Liberal Ward Com- mittee and a 1-trge number of independent Retepayers to allow myself to be nominated for a seat on the Town Council to represent Howley Ward, I have, after serious consideration, decided to place my services at. your die- posal. Having been In business in the Ward for over a quarter of a century, and taken an active interert in all matters affecting the welfare of the Ward, I think I can claim some small knowledge of your requirements. I may eay that I am both a large ratepayer and property owner in the Ward.so that I have some interest at stake. Unlike some aspirants to Municipal honours. I do not intend to make any rash and foolish promises ; but, if elected, you can rely upon me doing my utmost to forward the best interests of the Ratepayers. I an in favour of Lower Rates, Better Paved and Lighted streets and Passages, Cheaper Gas, and Batter Houses for the Working Classes. I am strongly in favour of providing a 2Zecreation Ground for the Children of the Ward, and would also like to see the wider streets planted with trees, so as o make the Ward rather more attractive than it has hitherto been. In conclusion, I can assure you, if honoured with your confidence, that my beet efforts will be devoted to secure the strictest possible economy in our Municipal Expeudt- tore coupled with Efficiency and Progress. I remain, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your Obedient servant, EDWARD PICKA.VANCE, 67, Bridge street, Warrington. ID. BAZAARS, t-hops, Markets, Hawkers.—Every 1. description of LI.
